blocks.html: $x^{2} - 2$ has no root in $\mathbb{Q}$, so we enlarge $\mathbb{Q}$ to a field that has one. There are two ways to do it, and they give the same field: adjoin $\sqrt{2}$ inside $\mathbb{R}$, or build the root out of nothing as a quotient ring.

Definitions. A field $K$ containing a field $F$ is an extension of $F$. For $\alpha \in K$, $F(\alpha)$ is the smallest subfield of $K$ containing $F$ and $\alpha$. Since $K$ is a vector space over $F$, the degree $[K : F]$ is its dimension.

Kronecker's construction. If $p(x)$ is irreducible over $F$ of degree $n$, then $K = F[x]/(p(x))$ is a field (the ideal $(p)$ is maximal), it contains a copy of $F$ (the constants), and the class $\alpha = x + (p)$ is a root of $p$, because $p(\alpha) = p(x) + (p) = 0$. Every element is a unique remainder $$a_{0} + a_{1}\alpha + \cdots + a_{n-1}\alpha^{n-1},$$ so $1, \alpha, \dots, \alpha^{n-1}$ is a basis and $[K : F] = n$. Multiplication: multiply as polynomials, then use $p(\alpha) = 0$. Inverses: by the Euclidean algorithm, or for square roots by the conjugate.

$\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ for $d$ not a perfect square is $\{a + b\sqrt{d} : a, b \in \mathbb{Q}\}$, which is $\mathbb{Q}[x]/(x^{2} - d)$. The inverse of $a + b\sqrt{d} \ne 0$ is $$\frac{a - b\sqrt{d}}{a^{2} - db^{2}},$$ where $a^{2} - db^{2} \ne 0$ because $\sqrt{d}$ is irrational.

blocks.title: Multiplying
blocks.q: In $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{3})$, compute $(1 + 2\sqrt{3})(3 - \sqrt{3})$.

blocks.title: Inverting
blocks.q: Write $\dfrac{1}{1 + 2\sqrt{3}}$ as $a + b\sqrt{3}$.
steps: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate $1 - 2\sqrt{3}$: the bottom becomes $1 - 4 \cdot 3 = -11$.

blocks.title: A cubic extension
blocks.q: Let $\theta = \sqrt[3]{2}$. In $\mathbb{Q}(\theta)$, compute $(1 + \theta)(\theta + \theta^{2})$.
steps: Every element of $\mathbb{Q}(\theta)$ is $a + b\theta + c\theta^{2}$, and $[\mathbb{Q}(\theta) : \mathbb{Q}] = 3$.

blocks.html: The same recipe gives $\mathbb{C} = \mathbb{R}[x]/(x^{2} + 1)$, with $i$ the class of $x$, and it gives the finite fields of the last two lessons.

Irreducible is essential. If $p$ factors, $F[x]/(p)$ is not a field: in $\mathbb{Q}[x]/(x^{2} - 1)$, the classes of $x - 1$ and $x + 1$ are nonzero, but their product is $0$. So a proof that $F[x]/(p)$ is a field starts by proving $p$ irreducible, with the tests of the last unit.

Inverting term by term: $\dfrac{1}{1 + 2\sqrt{3}}$ is not $1 + \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}$, just as $\frac{1}{1 + 2} \ne 1 + \frac{1}{2}$. Multiply by the conjugate, and check by multiplying back: the product must be exactly $1$.

For irreducible $p$ of degree $n$, $F[x]/(p)$ is a field of degree $n$ over $F$ containing a root $\alpha$, with basis $1, \alpha, \dots, \alpha^{n-1}$. In $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$, invert with the conjugate.

blocks.html: Many polynomials have $\sqrt{2}$ as a root: $x^{2} - 2$, $x^{4} - 4$, $x^{3} - 2x$. One of them is special: the smallest, and it tells you the size of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$. This lesson finds it in general and connects it to the degree of an extension.

Definitions. $\alpha$ (in an extension of $F$) is algebraic over $F$ if it is a root of some nonzero polynomial in $F[x]$. Its minimal polynomial is the monic polynomial of least degree with $\alpha$ as a root.

Theorem. The minimal polynomial $m(x)$ of $\alpha$ is irreducible, it divides every polynomial in $F[x]$ with root $\alpha$, and $[F(\alpha) : F] = \deg m$.
Proof. Divide any $f$ with $f(\alpha) = 0$ by $m$: $f = qm + r$ with $\deg r \lt \deg m$. Then $r(\alpha) = 0$, so $r = 0$ by minimality: $m \mid f$. If $m = gh$ with smaller degrees, then $g(\alpha)h(\alpha) = 0$ in a field, so one factor has root $\alpha$, contradicting minimality: $m$ is irreducible. Finally, $f \mapsto f(\alpha)$ sends $F[x]$ onto $F(\alpha)$ with kernel $(m)$, so $F(\alpha) \cong F[x]/(m)$, which has degree $\deg m$. $\square$ So: to find $[F(\alpha) : F]$, find any monic polynomial with root $\alpha$ and prove it irreducible.

blocks.title: A quadratic number
blocks.q: Find the minimal polynomial of $1 + \sqrt{3}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.
steps: $x^{2} - 2x - 2$ has no rational root ($\alpha$ is irrational), so it is irreducible.

blocks.title: A sum of square roots
blocks.q: Find the minimal polynomial of $\alpha = \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3}$.
steps: It is irreducible: $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ contains $\alpha^{2} = 5 + 2\sqrt{6}$, and also $\sqrt{2} = \frac{\alpha^{2} - 1}{2\alpha}$, so it is all of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3})$, which has degree $4$ (next lesson). A minimal polynomial of degree less than $4$ is impossible.

blocks.title: A cube root
blocks.q: Find the minimal polynomial of $\sqrt[3]{2} + 1$.
steps: It is irreducible: Eisenstein at $3$ applies ($3$ divides $-3, 3, -3$, not $1$, and $9 \nmid 3$).

blocks.html: The minimal polynomial depends on the base field. Over $\mathbb{Q}$, $\sqrt{2}$ has minimal polynomial $x^{2} - 2$; over $\mathbb{R}$, or over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$ itself, it is $x - \sqrt{2}$, of degree $1$.

Giving a polynomial with root $\alpha$ that factors. $x^{4} - 4$ has root $\sqrt{2}$, but $x^{4} - 4 = (x^{2} - 2)(x^{2} + 2)$, and the minimal polynomial is the factor $x^{2} - 2$. Before answering, check that your polynomial is monic and irreducible; its degree is then $[F(\alpha) : F]$.

The minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ is the monic irreducible polynomial with root $\alpha$; it divides every polynomial with root $\alpha$, and $F(\alpha) \cong F[x]/(m)$, so $[F(\alpha) : F] = \deg m$.

blocks.html: Degrees of field extensions multiply along a chain of fields, the same way dimensions would if you built a basis in two stages. This simple rule settles questions that puzzled mathematicians for two thousand years.

Tower law. If $F \subseteq K \subseteq L$ are fields with finite degrees, then $$[L : F] = [L : K]\,[K : F].$$ Proof. Let $u_{1}, \dots, u_{m}$ be a basis of $L$ over $K$ and $v_{1}, \dots, v_{n}$ a basis of $K$ over $F$. Every $x \in L$ is $\sum_{i} c_{i}u_{i}$ with $c_{i} \in K$, and each $c_{i} = \sum_{j} a_{ij}v_{j}$ with $a_{ij} \in F$; so the $mn$ products $u_{i}v_{j}$ span $L$ over $F$. If $\sum a_{ij}u_{i}v_{j} = 0$, group as $\sum_{i}(\sum_{j} a_{ij}v_{j})u_{i} = 0$: independence of the $u_{i}$ over $K$ makes each inner sum $0$, and independence of the $v_{j}$ over $F$ makes every $a_{ij} = 0$. So the $u_{i}v_{j}$ are a basis. $\square$

Consequence. If $\alpha \in L$, then $F \subseteq F(\alpha) \subseteq L$, so the degree of $\alpha$ divides $[L : F]$. For example, $\sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})$, because $2$ does not divide $3$.

blocks.name: aa-lattice
blocks.cap: The subfields of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3})$: three quadratic fields in the middle, each of degree 2 over $\mathbb{Q}$ and of degree 2 under the top.

blocks.title: Two square roots
blocks.q: Find $[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}) : \mathbb{Q}]$.
steps: Is $\sqrt{3} \in \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$? If $\sqrt{3} = a + b\sqrt{2}$ with rational $a, b$, squaring gives $3 = a^{2} + 2b^{2} + 2ab\sqrt{2}$, so $ab = 0$. If $b = 0$, $\sqrt{3} = a$ is rational; if $a = 0$, $\sqrt{3/2} = b$ is rational. Both are impossible.

blocks.title: Coprime degrees
blocks.q: Find $[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2}, \sqrt{3}) : \mathbb{Q}]$.
steps: $\sqrt[3]{2}$ has degree $3$ and $\sqrt{3}$ has degree $2$, and both divide the total degree, so $6$ divides it.
Adjoining $\sqrt{3}$ to $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})$ at most doubles the degree, so the total is at most $3 \cdot 2 = 6$.

blocks.title: Doubling the cube
blocks.q: Show that $\sqrt[3]{2}$ cannot be constructed with straightedge and compass.
steps: Each construction step solves at most a quadratic equation, so a constructible number lies in a tower $\mathbb{Q} = K_{0} \subset K_{1} \subset \cdots \subset K_{r}$ with each step of degree $2$; the top has degree $2^{r}$.
$\sqrt[3]{2}$ has degree $3$ (its minimal polynomial is $x^{3} - 2$), and $3$ does not divide $2^{r}$.
blocks.a: Not constructible: the ancient problem of doubling the cube is impossible.

blocks.html: Adding degrees instead of multiplying, or forgetting to check whether the new element is already in the field. $[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{8}) : \mathbb{Q}] = 2$, not $4$: $\sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}$ is already in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$, so the second step has degree $1$.

$[L : F] = [L : K][K : F]$: bases multiply. The degree of any element divides the degree of the field containing it; $[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}) : \mathbb{Q}] = 4$, and degree-3 numbers like $\sqrt[3]{2}$ are not constructible.

blocks.html: Codes on every phone and the ciphers behind secure web pages run on arithmetic in finite fields. Besides $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ there are fields of size $4, 8, 9, 16, 25, \dots$, built with the quotient-ring construction from polynomials over $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$.

Facts about finite fields.
(1) A finite field $F$ has prime characteristic $p$: the additive order of $1$ is finite, and if it were $ab$ with $a, b \gt 1$, then $(a \cdot 1)(b \cdot 1) = 0$ would give zero divisors. So $F$ contains a copy of $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$.
(2) $|F| = p^{n}$: $F$ is a vector space over $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ of some dimension $n$, and each vector has $n$ coordinates with $p$ choices each.
(3) For every prime power $p^{n}$ there is a field of that size, unique up to isomorphism, called $\mathrm{GF}(p^{n})$; it is $\mathbb{Z}_{p}[x]/(f)$ for any irreducible $f$ of degree $n$. (Existence and uniqueness are proved in Judson, chapter 22.)

Arithmetic in $\mathbb{Z}_{p}[x]/(f)$. Elements are polynomials of degree less than $n$ with coefficients mod $p$. Add coefficientwise. Multiply, then replace $x^{n}$ using $f = 0$. Invert with the Euclidean algorithm, or by search in small fields.

blocks.name: aa-gf
blocks.cap: $\mathrm{GF}(8) = \mathbb{Z}_{2}[x]/(x^{3} + x + 1)$. Every nonzero element is a power of $x$, so multiplying becomes adding exponents mod 7.

blocks.title: An inverse in $\mathrm{GF}(8)$
blocks.q: Find the inverse of $x + 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{2}[x]/(x^{3} + x + 1)$.

blocks.title: The field with 4 elements
blocks.q: Write the multiplication of $\mathrm{GF}(4) = \mathbb{Z}_{2}[x]/(x^{2} + x + 1)$.
blocks.a: The nonzero elements $1, x, x + 1$ form a cyclic group of order $3$.

blocks.html: The choice of $f$ does not matter. Over $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$, both $x^{3} + x + 1$ and $y^{3} + y^{2} + 1$ are irreducible, and both quotients are $\mathrm{GF}(8)$. An isomorphism sends $x$ to $y^{2} + y$, which is a root of $x^{3} + x + 1$ in the second field (check it).

Thinking $\mathrm{GF}(4)$ is $\mathbb{Z}_{4}$.
 In $\mathbb{Z}_{4}$, $2 \cdot 2 = 0$, so it is not a field. $\mathrm{GF}(4)$ has characteristic $2$ ($1 + 1 = 0$), and its elements are polynomials, not the numbers $0$ to $3$. The other common slip is forgetting to reduce by $f$ after multiplying: the answer must have degree less than $n$.

Every finite field has $p^{n}$ elements and characteristic $p$; $\mathrm{GF}(p^{n}) = \mathbb{Z}_{p}[x]/(f)$ for an irreducible $f$ of degree $n$. Compute with remainders: coefficients mod $p$, powers of $x$ reduced by $f = 0$.

blocks.html: In the last lesson, every nonzero element of $\mathrm{GF}(8)$ was a power of $x$. That is no accident: the multiplicative group of every finite field is cyclic. This is the fact behind discrete-logarithm cryptography and the log tables used to multiply in hardware.

Theorem. If $F$ is a finite field with $q$ elements, then $F^{*} = F \setminus \{0\}$ is a cyclic group of order $q - 1$.
Proof. For each $d \mid q - 1$ let $\psi(d)$ be the number of elements of order $d$ in $F^{*}$. If some $a$ has order $d$, then $1, a, \dots, a^{d-1}$ are $d$ different roots of $x^{d} - 1$, which has at most $d$ roots in a field; so the elements of order $d$ all lie in $\langle a \rangle$, a cyclic group with exactly $\varphi(d)$ of them. Hence $\psi(d)$ is $0$ or $\varphi(d)$. Now $\sum_{d} \psi(d) = q - 1 = \sum_{d} \varphi(d)$ (every element has some order; and the divisor sum of $\varphi$), so every $\psi(d) = \varphi(d)$. In particular $\psi(q - 1) = \varphi(q - 1) \ge 1$: there is an element of order $q - 1$. $\square$

A generator of $F^{*}$ is a primitive element; there are $\varphi(q - 1)$ of them. Two more facts: $\mathrm{GF}(p^{n})$ contains a subfield $\mathrm{GF}(p^{m})$ exactly when $m \mid n$ (for one direction, if $K \subseteq \mathrm{GF}(p^{n})$ has $p^{m}$ elements, the tower law over $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ gives $m \mid n$); and then that subfield is unique.

blocks.name: aa-gf
blocks.cap: $\mathrm{GF}(16) = \mathbb{Z}_{2}[x]/(x^{4} + x + 1)$: the powers of $x$ run through all 15 nonzero elements, so $x$ is primitive. The starred rows are the $\varphi(15) = 8$ primitive elements.

blocks.title: Is $x$ primitive?
blocks.q: In $\mathbb{Z}_{2}[x]/(x^{4} + x^{3} + x^{2} + x + 1)$, find the order of $x$.
steps: $5$ is prime and $x \ne 1$, so the order of $x$ is $5$, not $15$.
blocks.a: Order $5$: here $x$ is not primitive, though the quotient is still the field $\mathrm{GF}(16)$.

blocks.name: aa-gf
blocks.cap: The same field built from $x^{4} + x^{3} + x^{2} + x + 1$: the powers of $x$ repeat after 5 steps and miss ten nonzero elements.

blocks.title: Counting and subfields
blocks.q: How many primitive elements does $\mathrm{GF}(64)$ have, and which subfields does it contain?
steps: $F^{*}$ is cyclic of order $63$: $\varphi(63) = \varphi(9)\varphi(7) = 6 \cdot 6 = 36$ primitive elements.
$64 = 2^{6}$; the divisors of $6$ are $1, 2, 3, 6$, giving subfields of sizes $2, 4, 8, 64$.

blocks.html: Assuming $x$ is always primitive in $\mathbb{Z}_{p}[x]/(f)$; it depends on $f$, as the order-5 example shows. And "$\mathrm{GF}(2^{6})$ contains $\mathrm{GF}(2^{4})$ because $4 \lt 6$" is false: it needs $4 \mid 6$. Check the divisibility of the exponents, not their size.

The nonzero elements of $\mathrm{GF}(q)$ form a cyclic group of order $q - 1$ with $\varphi(q - 1)$ generators (primitive elements). $\mathrm{GF}(p^{n})$ contains $\mathrm{GF}(p^{m})$ exactly when $m \mid n$.

blocks.html: Abstract algebra studies operations themselves. You already know many: adding integers, multiplying matrices, adding and multiplying mod n, composing functions. This course asks what all of them have in common, so that one proof can cover every example at once. The first step is to say exactly what an operation is.

Definition. A binary operation on a set $S$ is a function $\ast: S \times S \to S$. It takes an ordered pair $(a, b)$ of elements of $S$ (an element of the Cartesian product $S \times S$) and returns one element $a \ast b$ that is again in $S$. That last requirement is called closure: subtraction is a binary operation on $\mathbb{Z}$, but not on $\mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$, because $1 - 2 \notin \mathbb{N}$.
For a small set we can list every answer in a Cayley table: the entry in row $a$ and column $b$ is $a \ast b$. The order matters, since $a \ast b$ and $b \ast a$ may differ.

blocks.name: aa-cayley

opts.task: Tap the cell for $4 + 2$ and then the cell for $2 + 4$. Are they equal?

blocks.cap: Addition mod 5 as a Cayley table. Each cell is tinted by its value, so you can see that every row and every column contains each element exactly once.

blocks.text: Properties you can read off (or not)

items: Commutative: $a \ast b = b \ast a$ for all $a, b$. In the table this means symmetry across the main diagonal.
Identity: an element $e$ with $e \ast a = a = a \ast e$ for all $a$. Its row and its column copy the headings.
Associative: $(a \ast b) \ast c = a \ast (b \ast c)$ for all $a, b, c$. This one is not visible in the table: for a set with $n$ elements there are $n^{3}$ triples to check.

blocks.html: Why care about associativity? It is what lets us drop parentheses and write $a \ast b \ast c \ast d$: every way of grouping gives the same answer. Without it, even $a \ast a \ast a$ is ambiguous. Every operation we build groups from will be associative, and the reason is usually that it comes from something already associative: addition and multiplication of numbers, multiplication of matrices, or composition of functions, where $(f \circ g) \circ h$ and $f \circ (g \circ h)$ both send $x$ to $f(g(h(x)))$.

blocks.title: Reading a table, both ways
blocks.q: On $S = \{a, b, c\}$ the table gives $a \ast b = c$ (row $a$, column $b$) and $b \ast a = a$ (row $b$, column $a$). Is $\ast$ commutative?
steps: Commutativity needs $x \ast y = y \ast x$ for every pair.
Here $a \ast b = c$ but $b \ast a = a$.

blocks.title: Testing associativity with a formula
blocks.q: On $\mathbb{Z}$ define $a \ast b = a + b + ab$. Is it associative?
steps: Notice $1 + (a \ast b) = 1 + a + b + ab = (1 + a)(1 + b)$.
So $1 + ((a \ast b) \ast c) = (1 + a)(1 + b)(1 + c)$, and the same for $1 + (a \ast (b \ast c))$.
Both groupings give the same number, because multiplication of integers is associative.

blocks.title: A commutative operation that is not associative
blocks.q: On $\mathbb{Z}$ define $a \ast b = |a - b|$. Check commutativity and associativity.
steps: $|a - b| = |b - a|$, so it is commutative.

blocks.html: Reading $b \ast a$ when you want $a \ast b$. The row is the left factor and the column is the right factor. A second trap: a symmetric table proves commutativity, not associativity. The example $|a - b|$ has a perfectly symmetric table and still fails associativity, so test triples, or find a reason like the $(1 + a)(1 + b)$ trick above.

A binary operation on $S$ sends each ordered pair of elements of $S$ to an element of $S$. A Cayley table lists all the answers (row $a$, column $b$ gives $a \ast b$); commutativity and identities show up in the table, but associativity has to be checked on triples or proved.

blocks.html: A group is the simplest structure in which every equation $a \ast x = b$ can be solved, the way you solve $3 + x = 7$ or $3x = 7$. Solving needs exactly three tools besides a binary operation: regrouping, a neutral element, and a way to undo.
Definition. A group is a set $G$ with a binary operation $\ast$ such that

items: (associativity) $(a \ast b) \ast c = a \ast (b \ast c)$ for all $a, b, c \in G$;
(identity) there is $e \in G$ with $e \ast a = a \ast e = a$ for all $a \in G$;
(inverses) for each $a \in G$ there is $a^{-1} \in G$ with $a \ast a^{-1} = a^{-1} \ast a = e$.

blocks.html: Closure is built into "binary operation on $G$", but when you test an example, check it first. A group is abelian if also $a \ast b = b \ast a$ always. The number of elements $|G|$ is the order of $G$. We usually write $ab$ for $a \ast b$; for abelian groups like $\mathbb{Z}$ we often write $a + b$, $0$ and $-a$ instead.

Here is why these axioms are the right ones. To solve $ax = b$, multiply on the left by $a^{-1}$: $$a^{-1}(ax) = a^{-1}b \;\Rightarrow\; (a^{-1}a)x = a^{-1}b \;\Rightarrow\; ex = a^{-1}b \;\Rightarrow\; x = a^{-1}b.$$ The steps use inverses, associativity, inverses again and the identity, in that order. Remove any axiom and some equation stops being solvable.

Group?

blocks.cap: Examples and non-examples. In the last row, $2x \equiv 1 \pmod 6$ has no solution, as you saw with modular inverses.

blocks.title: A finite group from a table
blocks.q: Is $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ a group under multiplication mod $5$?
steps: Closure: no product of two of these is a multiple of $5$, so every product lies in the set.
Associativity is inherited from multiplication of integers.
blocks.a: Yes. It is the group $U(5)$ of the next lesson.

blocks.title: A strange-looking group
blocks.q: On $\mathbb{Z}$ let $a \ast b = a + b + 1$. Find the identity and the inverse of $a$.
steps: Associativity: both $(a \ast b) \ast c$ and $a \ast (b \ast c)$ equal $a + b + c + 2$.
Identity: $a \ast u = a + u + 1 = a$ forces $u = -1$. Check: $(-1) \ast a = a$ too.

blocks.name: aa-cayley
blocks.cap: The group $U(10) = \{1, 3, 7, 9\}$ under multiplication mod 10. Each row contains the identity $1$ exactly once, in the column of that row's inverse.

blocks.html: Forgetting closure, or forgetting that every element needs an inverse. $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ under multiplication always fails, because $0 \cdot y = 0 \ne 1$; and when $n$ is not prime, numbers sharing a factor with $n$ fail too. Also remember that the inverse must combine with $a$ to give the identity of the operation, which need not be $0$ or $1$ (it was $-1$ above).

A group is a set with an associative operation, an identity, and an inverse for each element; closure must hold too. These are exactly the tools needed to solve $ax = b$, with the unique answer $x = a^{-1}b$.

blocks.html: Two families of groups come straight out of arithmetic mod n. They will be our most-used examples, because every computation in them is quick and exact.

The group $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$. The set $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ under addition mod $n$ is an abelian group of order $n$: the identity is $0$ and the inverse of $a$ is $n - a$ (and $-0 = 0$). Associativity comes from addition of integers.

The group $U(n)$. The set $$U(n) = \{a : 1 \le a \lt n,\ \gcd(a, n) = 1\}$$ under multiplication mod $n$ is an abelian group. Its order is Euler's $\varphi(n)$. For example $U(12) = \{1, 5, 7, 11\}$ and $U(7) = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$.

Why is $U(n)$ a group? Closure: if $\gcd(a, n) = \gcd(b, n) = 1$ and a prime $p$ divided both $ab$ and $n$, then $p$ would divide $a$ or $b$ (a prime dividing a product divides a factor), sharing a factor with $n$. So $\gcd(ab, n) = 1$, and reducing mod $n$ keeps that, since $\gcd(ab \bmod n, n) = \gcd(ab, n)$. Inverses: $\gcd(a, n) = 1$ gives integers with $ax + ny = 1$ (Bézout), so $ax \equiv 1$; reduce $x$ mod $n$, and it is coprime to $n$ too. These are the modular inverses you already know. Identity $1$, and associativity is inherited.

blocks.title: List a group of units
blocks.q: List $U(12)$ and compute its table.
steps: Keep the numbers below $12$ with no factor $2$ or $3$: $1, 5, 7, 11$.
Every element is its own inverse.

blocks.title: An inverse in $U(20)$
blocks.q: Find $7^{-1}$ in $U(20)$, then solve $7x = 9$ in $U(20)$.

blocks.name: aa-cayley
blocks.cap: The Cayley table of $U(12)$. The identity $1$ runs down the main diagonal: each element is its own inverse.

blocks.title: Inverses in $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$
blocks.q: In $\mathbb{Z}_{9}$, find $-4$ and solve $4 + x = 2$.

blocks.html: Mixing up the two groups. $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ uses addition (identity $0$); $U(n)$ uses multiplication (identity $1$) and contains only the residues coprime to $n$. Putting $2$ into $U(12)$ breaks the group: $2y \equiv 1 \pmod{12}$ has no solution, since $2y - 1$ is odd. A quick check: $a \in U(n)$ exactly when $\gcd(a, n) = 1$.

$\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ is $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ under addition mod $n$, of order $n$. $U(n)$ is the set of residues coprime to $n$ under multiplication mod $n$, of order $\varphi(n)$; inverses come from Bézout's identity.

blocks.html: Now we prove things from the group axioms alone. Every fact in this lesson then holds in every group at once: for integers, matrices, permutations and symmetries alike. The proofs are short, and they show the habits of a good proof: name your objects, justify each equals sign by an axiom or an earlier result, and end exactly at the claim.

blocks.text: The identity and inverses are unique

blocks.html:
Theorem. A group has exactly one identity, and each element has exactly one inverse.
Proof. Suppose $e$ and $e'$ are both identities. Then $e = ee'$ (because $e'$ is an identity) and $ee' = e'$ (because $e$ is an identity), so $e = e'$.
Suppose $b$ and $c$ are both inverses of $a$. Then $$b = be = b(ac) = (ba)c = ec = c,$$ using in turn: $e$ is the identity, $ac = e$, associativity, $ba = e$, and the identity again. $\square$
Because inverses are unique, to show that some $y$ is the inverse of $x$, it is enough to check $xy = e$. (From $xy = e$, multiply on the left by $x^{-1}$ to get $y = x^{-1}$.)
Theorem. If $ab = ac$ then $b = c$, and if $ba = ca$ then $b = c$. The equations $ax = b$ and $xa = b$ have the unique solutions $x = a^{-1}b$ and $x = ba^{-1}$.

Proof of left cancellation. Multiply $ab = ac$ on the left by $a^{-1}$: $a^{-1}(ab) = a^{-1}(ac)$. By associativity $(a^{-1}a)b = (a^{-1}a)c$, so $eb = ec$ and $b = c$. $\square$ A consequence you can see: in a Cayley table, each row and each column contains every element exactly once.

Theorem. $(ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}$, and $(a^{-1})^{-1} = a$.
Proof. By associativity, $(ab)(b^{-1}a^{-1}) = a(bb^{-1})a^{-1} = aea^{-1} = aa^{-1} = e$, so $b^{-1}a^{-1}$ is the inverse of $ab$. And $a^{-1}a = e$ says $a$ is the inverse of $a^{-1}$. $\square$ Think of socks and shoes: you put on socks, then shoes, and take them off in the reverse order.

blocks.title: Socks and shoes with matrices
blocks.q: In the group of $2 \times 2$ integer matrices with determinant $1$, let $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Find $(AB)^{-1}$.
steps: The other order, $A^{-1}B^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, is the inverse of $BA$, not of $AB$.

blocks.title: A short proof
blocks.q: Prove: if $x^{2} = e$ for every $x$ in a group $G$, then $G$ is abelian.
steps: Let $a, b \in G$. Since $x^{2} = e$ means $x = x^{-1}$, every element is its own inverse.
So $ab = (ab)^{-1}$, because $ab$ is an element too.

blocks.html: Writing $(ab)^{-1} = a^{-1}b^{-1}$. That would need $ba^{-1} = a^{-1}b$, which is only true when $a$ and $b$ commute; the matrix example shows it failing. Another slip: cancelling on opposite sides. From $ab = ca$ you can only conclude $c = aba^{-1}$, not $b = c$. To check a proof, ask of each equals sign: which axiom, applied on which side?

From the axioms alone: the identity and inverses are unique, you may cancel on the same side ($ab = ac \Rightarrow b = c$), $ax = b$ has the unique solution $x = a^{-1}b$, and $(ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}$.

blocks.html: In number theory the order of $a$ mod $n$ was the first power of $a$ that is $1$. The same idea works in every group, and it is the most useful single number attached to an element.

Definition. The order of $a$, written $|a|$, is the least positive integer $n$ with $a^{n} = e$. If no such $n$ exists, $a$ has infinite order. In additive notation the condition reads $na = a + a + \cdots + a = 0$.

Here $a^{n}$ means $a$ multiplied by itself $n$ times, $a^{0} = e$, and $a^{-n} = (a^{-1})^{n}$; the usual rules $a^{m}a^{n} = a^{m+n}$ and $(a^{m})^{n} = a^{mn}$ hold in any group (by associativity), while $(ab)^{n} = a^{n}b^{n}$ needs $ab = ba$.

Theorem. If $|a| = n$, then $a^{k} = e$ exactly when $n$ divides $k$.
Proof. If $k = nq$ then $a^{k} = (a^{n})^{q} = e^{q} = e$. Conversely, suppose $a^{k} = e$ and divide: $k = nq + r$ with $0 \le r < n$. Then $$e = a^{k} = (a^{n})^{q}a^{r} = a^{r}.$$ Since $n$ is the least positive exponent giving $e$ and $0 \le r < n$, we must have $r = 0$, so $n \mid k$. $\square$ Consequence: $a^{i} = a^{j}$ exactly when $i \equiv j \pmod{n}$, so exponents can be reduced mod $|a|$. In particular the powers $e, a, a^{2}, \dots, a^{n-1}$ are all different: if two of them agreed, a smaller positive power would already be $e$.

steps: We need the least $m \ge 1$ with $6m \equiv 0 \pmod{16}$, that is, $16 \mid 6m$, that is, $8 \mid 3m$.

blocks.title: Order in $U(10)$
blocks.q: Find the order of $3$ in $U(10)$.
blocks.a: $|3| = 4$, which equals $|U(10)|$, so the powers of $3$ fill $U(10)$.

blocks.q: Find the order of $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, the rotation by $90^\circ$.
steps: $A^{4} = (A^{2})^{2} = I$, and no smaller power is $I$.

The two agree only for an element that generates the whole group. Another slip: in $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ the operation is addition, so the order of $6$ comes from $6 + 6 + \cdots$, not from $6 \cdot 6 \cdot \cdots$.
$|a|$ is the least $n \ge 1$ with $a^{n} = e$ (or $na = 0$ additively). Then $a^{k} = e$ exactly when $|a|$ divides $k$, and exponents can be reduced mod $|a|$.

blocks.html: Many groups live inside bigger ones: the even integers inside $\mathbb{Z}$, the rotations inside all symmetries of a square, the matrices of determinant $1$ inside all invertible matrices, and smaller groups of units inside the groups $U(n)$. Studying these pieces is the main way we take a group apart.
Definition. A subset $H$ of a group $G$ is a subgroup, written $H \le G$, if $H$ is a group under the operation of $G$. Every group has the subgroups $\{e\}$ and $G$.
Associativity is inherited automatically, so only three things need checking: $H$ contains $e$, $H$ is closed under the operation, and $H$ is closed under inverses. These can be packed into one test.

One-step subgroup test. If $H \subseteq G$ is nonempty and $ab^{-1} \in H$ whenever $a, b \in H$, then $H \le G$.
Proof. Pick $h \in H$. Then $e = hh^{-1} \in H$. For $b \in H$, $b^{-1} = eb^{-1} \in H$. For $a, b \in H$ we now know $b^{-1} \in H$, so $ab = a(b^{-1})^{-1} \in H$. Associativity holds in $H$ because it holds in $G$. $\square$

Finite subgroup test. If $H$ is finite and nonempty, closure alone is enough. The reason: for $a \in H$, the powers $a, a^{2}, a^{3}, \dots$ all lie in $H$, so two of them are equal, $a^{i} = a^{j}$ with $i < j$; cancelling gives $a^{j-i} = e$. Then $e \in H$ and $a^{-1} = a^{j-i-1} \in H$.

blocks.title: A subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$
blocks.q: Is $H = \{0, 3, 6, 9\}$ a subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$?
steps: $H$ is finite, so check closure under addition mod $12$.
Every sum of multiples of $3$ is a multiple of $3$, and reducing mod $12$ keeps it a multiple of $3$ (since $3 \mid 12$).

blocks.title: A subgroup of $U(15)$
steps: All products stay in $H$, and $H$ is finite.

blocks.cap: $U(15)$ with $H = \{1, 4, 11, 14\}$ lit. The block where both the row and the column are in $H$ uses only elements of $H$: that is closure.

blocks.title: Matrices of determinant 1
blocks.q: Show that $SL_{2}(\mathbb{R})$, the real $2 \times 2$ matrices with determinant $1$, is a subgroup of the invertible matrices.
steps: It contains $I$, so it is nonempty.
For $A, B$ in it, $\det(AB^{-1}) = \det A / \det B = 1/1 = 1$.
By the one-step test, it is a subgroup.

blocks.html: Checking closure but not inverses for an infinite set. $\mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ is closed under addition, yet it is not a subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}$: $1$ has no inverse in $\mathbb{N}$. The shortcut "closure is enough" works only for finite subsets. Also check for the identity early: the odd integers fail at once, since $0$ is not odd.
$H \le G$ when $H$ is a group under $G$'s operation. Test: $H$ nonempty and $ab^{-1} \in H$ for all $a, b \in H$; for finite $H$, closure alone suffices.

blocks.html: The simplest way to build a subgroup is to start from one element and take everything it forces you to include. If $a \in H$, then all of $a, a^{2}, a^{3}, \dots$, $e$ and $a^{-1}, a^{-2}, \dots$ must be in $H$ too.

Definition. The cyclic subgroup generated by $a$ is $$\langle a \rangle = \{a^{k} : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$$ (in additive notation $\langle a \rangle = \{ka : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$). A group $G$ is cyclic if $G = \langle a \rangle$ for some $a$, called a generator.

$\langle a \rangle$ is a subgroup, and the smallest one containing $a$. It contains $a^{0} = e$, and $a^{j}(a^{k})^{-1} = a^{j-k}$ is again a power of $a$, so the one-step test passes. Any subgroup containing $a$ contains every power of $a$, so it contains $\langle a \rangle$. And if $|a| = n$, the order lesson showed that $e, a, \dots, a^{n-1}$ are distinct and every power equals one of them: so $|\langle a \rangle| = |a|$.

Cyclic groups are always abelian, since $a^{j}a^{k} = a^{j+k} = a^{k}a^{j}$. Examples: $\mathbb{Z} = \langle 1 \rangle$; $\mathbb{Z}_{n} = \langle 1 \rangle$; the rotations of a regular $n$-gon, generated by the smallest rotation; the $n$th roots of unity in $\mathbb{C}$, generated by $e^{2\pi i/n}$.

blocks.name: complexplane
blocks.cap: The sixth roots of unity. Multiplying by $e^{2\pi i/6}$ turns the picture by $60^\circ$, so its powers visit all six points: a cyclic group of order 6, just like $\mathbb{Z}_{6}$.

blocks.html:
Theorem. $k$ generates $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ exactly when $\gcd(k, n) = 1$. Hence $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ has $\varphi(n)$ generators.
Proof. If $\langle k \rangle = \mathbb{Z}_{n}$, then $1 \in \langle k \rangle$, so $kx \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$ for some $x$, and then $\gcd(k, n) = 1$. Conversely, if $\gcd(k, n) = 1$, Bézout gives $kx + ny = 1$, so $1 = xk$ lies in $\langle k \rangle$, and then every $m = m \cdot 1$ does. $\square$

blocks.title: Generators of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$
blocks.q: List the generators of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$, and describe $\langle 8 \rangle$.
steps: $\langle 8 \rangle$: $8, 16 \equiv 4, 12 \equiv 0$, then it repeats. So $\langle 8 \rangle = \{0, 4, 8\}$, of order $3 = |8|$.

blocks.title: Is $U(10)$ cyclic? Is $U(8)$?
blocks.q: Decide whether $U(10)$ and $U(8)$ are cyclic.
steps: $U(10) = \{1, 3, 7, 9\}$: powers of $3$ are $3, 9, 7, 1$, all four elements. So $U(10) = \langle 3 \rangle$ is cyclic.
$U(8) = \{1, 3, 5, 7\}$: $3^{2} = 9 \equiv 1$, $5^{2} = 25 \equiv 1$, $7^{2} = 49 \equiv 1$. Every element has order at most $2$, so none generates a group of order $4$.

blocks.html: Two wrong guesses. "The generators of $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ are the primes below $n$": in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ the prime $3$ is not a generator ($\langle 3 \rangle = \{0, 3, 6, 9\}$), while $1$, which is not prime, is one. The test is $\gcd(k, n) = 1$. And "abelian means cyclic": $U(8)$ is abelian, but every element squares to $1$, so no single element generates it.

$\langle a \rangle = \{a^{k}\}$ is the smallest subgroup containing $a$, and it has $|a|$ elements. $G$ is cyclic when one element generates it; $k$ generates $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ exactly when $\gcd(k, n) = 1$.

blocks.html: If you know the order of $a$, you know the order of every power of $a$, with one gcd. This formula drives everything about cyclic groups.

Theorem. If $|a| = n$ and $k$ is an integer, then $$|a^{k}| = \frac{n}{\gcd(n, k)}.$$ Proof. Let $d = \gcd(n, k)$. By the order lemma, $(a^{k})^{m} = a^{km} = e$ exactly when $n \mid km$. Divide by $d$: $n \mid km$ exactly when $\frac{n}{d} \mid \frac{k}{d}m$. Now $\frac{n}{d}$ and $\frac{k}{d}$ share no factor, so this happens exactly when $\frac{n}{d} \mid m$. The least positive such $m$ is $\frac{n}{d}$. $\square$

Look at the shape of that proof, because it recurs all course: turn the statement about the group into a divisibility statement with the order lemma ($a^{j} = e \iff n \mid j$), then finish with plain number theory. Nothing about the particular group was used, so the formula holds in $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$, in $U(n)$, for rotations, for matrices.
In $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$, where $k = k \cdot 1$ and $|1| = n$, the formula says the element $k$ has order $n/\gcd(n, k)$. Two consequences:

items: $\langle a^{k} \rangle = \langle a^{\gcd(n, k)} \rangle$: both have $n/\gcd(n, k)$ elements, and $a^{k}$ is a power of $a^{\gcd(n,k)}$, so the first sits inside the second, with the same size.
$a^{k}$ generates $\langle a \rangle$ exactly when $\gcd(n, k) = 1$; and $a^{i}$, $a^{j}$ generate the same subgroup exactly when $\gcd(n, i) = \gcd(n, j)$.

steps: $\gcd(30, 18) = 6$ too, so $|a^{18}| = 5$, and in fact $\langle a^{12} \rangle = \langle a^{18} \rangle = \langle a^{6} \rangle$.

blocks.html: Cyclic groups have the tidiest subgroups of any groups: you can list all of them from the divisors of the order. This uses the orders of powers and one division with remainder.

Theorem. Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic.
Proof. Let $G = \langle a \rangle$ and $H \le G$. If $H = \{e\}$, it is $\langle e \rangle$. Otherwise $H$ contains some $a^{k}$ with $k \ne 0$, and then also $a^{-k}$, so it contains a positive power of $a$. Let $m$ be the smallest positive integer with $a^{m} \in H$. Take any $a^{k} \in H$ and divide: $k = mq + r$ with $0 \le r \lt m$. Then $$a^{r} = a^{k}(a^{m})^{-q} \in H,$$ because $H$ is closed under products and inverses. Since $r \lt m$ and $m$ was smallest, $r = 0$. So $a^{k} = (a^{m})^{q}$, and $H = \langle a^{m} \rangle$. $\square$

Theorem (subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$). For each positive divisor $d$ of $n$, $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ has exactly one subgroup of order $d$, namely $\langle n/d \rangle$, and these are all its subgroups.
Why. Each subgroup is $\langle k \rangle = \langle \gcd(n, k) \rangle$, generated by a divisor $g$ of $n$, of order $n/g$. Different divisors give different orders, so there is one subgroup per order.

Counting elements by order: the elements of order $d$ are exactly the generators of the subgroup of order $d$, a cyclic group of order $d$, so there are $\varphi(d)$ of them. Adding over all divisors gives the identity $\sum_{d \mid n} \varphi(d) = n$. For $n = 12$: $\varphi(1) + \varphi(2) + \varphi(3) + \varphi(4) + \varphi(6) + \varphi(12) = 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 4 = 12$.

The infinite cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}$ works the same way: by the theorem, every subgroup is $\langle m \rangle = m\mathbb{Z}$, the multiples of a single $m \ge 0$. You will meet these again as the ideals of the ring $\mathbb{Z}$.

Subgroups of cyclic groups are cyclic. $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ has exactly one subgroup of each order $d \mid n$, namely $\langle n/d \rangle$, and exactly $\varphi(d)$ elements of order $d$.

blocks.html: Subgroups are ordered by inclusion, a partial order, so we can draw them as a Hasse diagram: bigger subgroups higher, with a line when one sits directly inside another. This picture is called the subgroup lattice.

For $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ the subgroups are $\langle d \rangle$ for the divisors $d$ of $n$, and $$\langle d \rangle \subseteq \langle d' \rangle \iff d' \mid d,$$ because $\langle d \rangle$ is the set of multiples of $d$. So the lattice of $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ is the divisor diagram of $n$ turned upside down: $\langle 1 \rangle = \mathbb{Z}_{n}$ at the top, $\langle n \rangle = \{0\}$ at the bottom.

To draw it by hand, put $\{0\}$ at the bottom and climb one prime at a time: from $\langle d \rangle$ you can step up to $\langle d/p \rangle$ for each prime $p$ dividing $d$. Every edge then has index $p$, a prime, and the subgroups at each height have the same number of prime factors in their index.

blocks.name: aa-lattice
blocks.cap: The subgroup lattice of $\mathbb{Z}_{24}$. Tap $\langle 4 \rangle$: above it are $\langle 2 \rangle$ and $\langle 1 \rangle$ (generators that divide 4), and inside it are $\langle 8 \rangle$, $\langle 12 \rangle$ and $\{0\}$. The numbers on the edges are indices.

blocks.html: For divisors $a$ and $b$ of $n$: $$\langle a \rangle \cap \langle b \rangle = \langle \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) \rangle, \qquad \text{the smallest subgroup containing both} = \langle \gcd(a, b) \rangle.$$ The intersection is the set of common multiples of $a$ and $b$, which are the multiples of the lcm. A subgroup containing $a$ and $b$ contains every $sa + tb$, and by Bézout those are the multiples of $\gcd(a, b)$. In the diagram these are the highest point below both and the lowest point above both.

steps: $\gcd(6, 9) = 3$, so the smallest subgroup containing both is $\langle 3 \rangle$, of order $12$.

blocks.q: Which subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_{24}$ sit directly above $\langle 12 \rangle$?
steps: $\langle d \rangle \supsetneq \langle 12 \rangle$ means $d$ is a proper divisor of $12$.
Nothing lies in between when $12/d$ is prime: $d = 6$ ($12/6 = 2$) and $d = 4$ ($12/4 = 3$).

blocks.html: Groups that are not cyclic have richer lattices. $\mathbb{Z}_{4}$ has a single subgroup of order $2$, but $U(8) = \{1, 3, 5, 7\}$, also of order $4$, has three: $\{1, 3\}$, $\{1, 5\}$ and $\{1, 7\}$. The symmetries of a square, $D_{4}$, have ten subgroups.

The subgroup lattice shows inclusion. For $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$, $\langle d \rangle \subseteq \langle d' \rangle$ exactly when $d' \mid d$; intersections come from lcms and joins from gcds.

blocks.html: A permutation is a rearrangement, and rearrangements were the first groups ever studied: Lagrange and Galois looked at how the roots of a polynomial can be shuffled. Formally a permutation is a bijection from a set to itself.

Definition. $S_{n}$ is the set of all bijections $\sigma: \{1, \dots, n\} \to \{1, \dots, n\}$, with composition as the operation. It has $n!$ elements. We write $\sigma$ in two-row notation, with each number above its image: $$\sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$ means $\sigma(1) = 2$, $\sigma(2) = 3$, $\sigma(3) = 1$.

$S_{n}$ is a group. A composition of bijections is a bijection (closure). Composition of functions is associative: $(\sigma \circ \tau) \circ \rho$ and $\sigma \circ (\tau \circ \rho)$ both send $x$ to $\sigma(\tau(\rho(x)))$. The identity map is the identity, and the inverse function $\sigma^{-1}$ (read the two rows bottom to top) is the inverse.

Our convention. $\sigma\tau$ means $\sigma \circ \tau$: do $\tau$ first, then $\sigma$, exactly as for functions, $(\sigma\tau)(x) = \sigma(\tau(x))$. (Some books compose left to right; always check.)

blocks.q: Find the inverse of $\sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 3 & 1 & 4 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$.
steps: Sort the columns by the top row: $\sigma^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$.
Check: $\sigma(\sigma^{-1}(1)) = \sigma(2) = 1$, and so on for each number.

blocks.html: Counting: to build a permutation, choose $\sigma(1)$ ($n$ ways), then $\sigma(2)$ ($n - 1$ ways), and so on, giving $n!$. So $|S_{3}| = 6$, $|S_{4}| = 24$, $|S_{5}| = 120$: these groups grow fast.

Permutation groups matter far beyond shuffling. Later in the course, Cayley's theorem shows that every group can be pictured as a group of permutations, so the habits you build here (follow one input at a time, read right to left) work for every group you will meet.

Composing left to right. With our convention, $\sigma\tau$ applies $\tau$ first. To check a product, follow one input all the way: start at $1$, apply the right-hand factor, then the left-hand one. If your answer for $(\sigma\tau)(1)$ matches $\sigma(\tau(1))$, the order is right.

$S_{n}$ is the group of all $n!$ permutations of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ under composition. $\sigma\tau$ means "do $\tau$, then $\sigma$"; inverses come from swapping the two rows; for $n \ge 3$ the group is not abelian.

blocks.html: Two-row notation lists every number, even the ones that do not move. Permutations have a much shorter description: follow each number around until it comes back.

Cycles. The cycle $(a_{1}\;a_{2}\;\dots\;a_{k})$ sends $a_{1} \to a_{2} \to \cdots \to a_{k} \to a_{1}$ and fixes every other number. It has length $k$; a 2-cycle is a transposition. The same cycle can start anywhere: $(1\;4\;3) = (4\;3\;1) = (3\;1\;4)$.

Every permutation is a product of disjoint cycles, in exactly one way (apart from the order of the cycles and where each one starts). Algorithm: start at the smallest number, $1$, and follow $1 \to \sigma(1) \to \sigma(\sigma(1)) \to \cdots$. Since there are finitely many numbers and $\sigma$ is one-to-one, you must come back to $1$ (you cannot return to a middle number first, because it already has its preimage in the chain). Close the cycle, then start again at the smallest unused number. Fixed points form cycles of length $1$, which we leave out.

blocks.html: Disjoint cycles commute: they move different numbers, so it does not matter which acts first. Cycles that share a number usually do not commute, and a product of overlapping cycles must be multiplied out, right to left like any composition.

steps: $1$: the right cycle fixes $1$, the left sends $1 \to 2$. So $1 \mapsto 2$.

steps: Run each cycle backward: $(1\;5\;2\;4)^{-1} = (4\;2\;5\;1) = (1\;4\;2\;5)$, and a transposition is its own inverse.
The cycles are disjoint, so invert them one at a time.

blocks.html: Treating overlapping cycles as if they were disjoint. $(1\;2\;3)(2\;3\;4)$ is not "a 3-cycle and a 3-cycle"; multiplied out it is $(1\;2)(3\;4)$. And multiply right to left: done left to right, the same product would give $(1\;3)(2\;4)$. A good check is to trace a single number through the cycles in both orders and see which matches the definition $\sigma\tau = \sigma \circ \tau$.

Every permutation is a product of disjoint cycles, found by following $1 \to \sigma(1) \to \cdots$ until you return. Disjoint cycles commute; overlapping cycles are multiplied right to left; inverses run each cycle backward.

blocks.html: With cycle notation, the order of a permutation can be read off with no multiplying at all.

Theorem. The order of a permutation written as a product of disjoint cycles of lengths $k_{1}, \dots, k_{r}$ is $\operatorname{lcm}(k_{1}, \dots, k_{r})$.
Proof. A $k$-cycle has order $k$: each application moves every entry one place around the cycle, and they all come back to the start for the first time after $k$ steps. Disjoint cycles commute, so $$(\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}\cdots\gamma_{r})^{m} = \gamma_{1}^{m}\gamma_{2}^{m}\cdots\gamma_{r}^{m},$$ and since the cycles move different numbers, this is the identity exactly when each $\gamma_{i}^{m}$ is, that is, when every $k_{i}$ divides $m$. The least such $m$ is the lcm. $\square$

blocks.cap: $(1\;2\;3)(4\;5)$: the 3-cycle returns after 3 steps and the 2-cycle after 2, so everything returns together after $\operatorname{lcm}(3, 2) = 6$ steps.

blocks.title: Overlapping cycles first
blocks.q: Find the order of $(1\;2)(2\;3)$.
steps: The cycles overlap, so multiply first: $3 \to 2 \to 1$, $1 \to 1 \to 2$, $2 \to 3 \to 3$, giving $(1\;2\;3)$.
(The lcm of the original lengths, $2$, would be wrong.)

blocks.html: The lengths of the disjoint cycles (with fixed points as cycles of length 1) form the cycle type. To count the permutations of a given type in $S_{n}$, fill the pattern with the $n$ numbers and divide out the repeats: each $k$-cycle can be written starting at any of its $k$ entries, and cycles of equal length can be listed in any order. With $m_{k}$ cycles of length $k$ (including $k = 1$): $$\#\{\text{permutations of that type}\} = \frac{n!}{\prod_{k} k^{m_{k}}\, m_{k}!}.$$

blocks.title: Counting 3-cycles in $S_{5}$
blocks.q: How many 3-cycles does $S_{5}$ contain?

blocks.title: A big power
steps: The order is $\operatorname{lcm}(3, 4) = 12$, so exponents work mod $12$: $100 = 12 \cdot 8 + 4$, and $\sigma^{100} = \sigma^{4}$.
Powers of disjoint cycles can be taken one cycle at a time: $(1\;2\;3)^{4} = (1\;2\;3)$ and $(4\;5\;6\;7)^{4} = e$.

blocks.html: Adding or multiplying cycle lengths instead of taking their lcm: $(1\;2\;3\;4)(5\;6)$ has order $\operatorname{lcm}(4, 2) = 4$, not $6$ or $8$. And take the lcm only after rewriting as disjoint cycles; overlapping ones can merge into longer cycles or cancel.
For disjoint cycles, the order of the product is the lcm of the cycle lengths. The cycle type also tells how many permutations look alike: $n!/\prod k^{m_{k}} m_{k}!$.

blocks.html: Every shuffle of a deck can be done by swapping two cards at a time. In the language of cycles: every permutation is a product of transpositions. The surprise is that the number of swaps, though not fixed, is always even or always odd for a given permutation.

Transpositions generate $S_{n}$. A $k$-cycle is a product of $k - 1$ transpositions: $$(a_{1}\;a_{2}\;\dots\;a_{k}) = (a_{1}\;a_{k})(a_{1}\;a_{k-1})\cdots(a_{1}\;a_{3})(a_{1}\;a_{2}),$$ multiplied right to left as usual. For example $(1\;2\;3\;4) = (1\;4)(1\;3)(1\;2)$. Since every permutation is a product of cycles, it is a product of transpositions.

Theorem. A permutation cannot be both a product of an even number and of an odd number of transpositions.
Proof. For $\sigma \in S_{n}$, let $c(\sigma)$ be its number of cycles, counting fixed points as 1-cycles, and let $N(\sigma) = n - c(\sigma)$; the identity has $N = 0$. Multiplying by a transposition $(a\;b)$ changes $c$ by exactly one: if $a$ and $b$ lie in the same cycle, that cycle splits in two; if they lie in different cycles, the two merge. So each transposition changes the parity of $N$. A product of $m$ transpositions therefore has $N \equiv m \pmod{2}$, and the parity of $m$ is fixed by $\sigma$ alone. $\square$

So we may define the sign: $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) = +1$ if $\sigma$ is even (an even number of transpositions) and $-1$ if odd. From the cycle formula, a $k$-cycle has sign $(-1)^{k-1}$: odd-length cycles are even. Signs multiply: $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma\tau) = \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\operatorname{sgn}(\tau)$, because the transposition counts add.

The alternating group. The even permutations form a subgroup $A_{n}$ (the identity is even, and products and inverses of even permutations are even). For $n \ge 2$, multiplying by $(1\;2)$ swaps the even and odd permutations one for one, so exactly half are even: $|A_{n}| = n!/2$.

Counts: $1$ identity, $4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2/3 = 8$ three-cycles, and $3$ double transpositions $(1\;2)(3\;4)$, $(1\;3)(2\;4)$, $(1\;4)(2\;3)$.

blocks.html: Calling a 3-cycle odd "because 3 is odd". The sign of a $k$-cycle is $(-1)^{k-1}$: count the $k - 1$ transpositions, not the $k$ entries. So 3-cycles are even and 2-cycles (transpositions) are odd.
Every permutation is a product of transpositions, always an even number or always an odd number of them. A $k$-cycle is even when $k$ is odd. The even permutations form $A_{n}$, with $n!/2$ elements.

blocks.html: A regular polygon can be moved onto itself in exactly $2n$ ways, and these motions form a group. It is the main example of a nonabelian group you can hold in your hands, and it connects the symmetry you met in geometry with permutations.

Definition. $D_{n}$ ($n \ge 3$) is the group of symmetries of a regular $n$-gon, under composition. Number the vertices $1, \dots, n$ counterclockwise. Let $r$ be the rotation by $360^\circ/n$ counterclockwise, and let $s$ be the reflection in the line through vertex $1$ and the center. (Some books call this group $D_{2n}$, after its order.)

The elements. A symmetry is fixed by where it sends vertex 1 (one of $n$ places) and whether it keeps or reverses the order of the labels around the polygon (2 choices), so $|D_{n}| = 2n$. They are the $n$ rotations $e, r, r^{2}, \dots, r^{n-1}$ and the $n$ reflections $s, rs, r^{2}s, \dots, r^{n-1}s$.

The rule $sr = r^{-1}s$. Reflecting reverses the direction of turning. Check where vertex 1 goes: $r$ sends it to position 2, then $s$ sends position 2 to position $n$. And $r^{-1}s$: $s$ fixes vertex 1, then $r^{-1}$ sends it to position $n$. Both are reflections that agree on vertex 1, so they are equal. Repeating gives $sr^{k} = r^{-k}s$. Together with $r^{n} = e$ and $s^{2} = e$, this rule lets you push every $s$ to the right and write any product as $r^{k}$ or $r^{k}s$ with $0 \le k \lt n$.

blocks.html: A subgroup $H$ cuts its group into equal pieces. You have seen this already: the residue classes mod $4$ are the pieces of $\mathbb{Z}$ cut out by $4\mathbb{Z}$. The pieces are called cosets, and they are the key to the next three topics.

Definition. For $H \le G$ and $a \in G$, the left coset of $H$ containing $a$ is $$aH = \{ah : h \in H\}.$$ The right coset is $Ha = \{ha : h \in H\}$. In additive notation we write $a + H$. For example, in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ with $H = \langle 4 \rangle = \{0, 4, 8\}$, the coset $1 + H = \{1, 5, 9\}$.

The cosets of $H$ split $G$ into disjoint pieces of size $|H|$.
(1) They cover $G$: $a = ae \in aH$.
(2) Two cosets are equal or disjoint: define $a \sim b$ when $a^{-1}b \in H$. This is an equivalence relation: $a^{-1}a = e \in H$; if $a^{-1}b \in H$ then its inverse $b^{-1}a \in H$; if $a^{-1}b, b^{-1}c \in H$ then their product $a^{-1}c \in H$. The class of $a$ is $\{b : b = ah \text{ for some } h \in H\} = aH$, and equivalence classes are equal or disjoint. In particular $$aH = bH \iff a^{-1}b \in H.$$
(3) Same size: the map $h \mapsto ah$ from $H$ to $aH$ is onto by definition and one-to-one by cancellation ($ah = ah' \Rightarrow h = h'$). $\square$

$aH = \{ah : h \in H\}$. The left cosets of $H$ partition $G$ into pieces of size $|H|$, and $aH = bH$ exactly when $a^{-1}b \in H$.

blocks.html: Since the cosets of $H$ are equal-size pieces that fill up $G$, counting them gives one of the most useful theorems in algebra.

Lagrange's theorem. If $G$ is finite and $H \le G$, then $|H|$ divides $|G|$, and the number of left cosets is $$[G : H] = \frac{|G|}{|H|}.$$ Proof. The left cosets of $H$ are disjoint and cover $G$, and each has exactly $|H|$ elements (the map $h \mapsto ah$ is a bijection $H \to aH$). If there are $k$ of them, then $|G| = k\,|H|$. So $|H|$ divides $|G|$, and $k = |G|/|H|$. $\square$
The number $[G : H]$ is the index of $H$ in $G$. Indices multiply along a chain $K \le H \le G$: $[G : K] = [G : H]\,[H : K]$, since $\frac{|G|}{|K|} = \frac{|G|}{|H|} \cdot \frac{|H|}{|K|}$.
Look at the shape of that proof: a partition into equal pieces turns a structure question into arithmetic. You will see the same move again in the orbit–stabilizer theorem.

steps: For order $15$: $1, 3, 5, 15$. A group of order $15$ has no subgroup of order $2$, $4$ or $6$.

blocks.html: Lagrange says subgroup orders must divide $|G|$. It does not say every divisor occurs. The classic example is $A_{4}$, of order $12$, which has no subgroup of order $6$. A subgroup of order $6$ would have index $2$; you will see that such a subgroup contains the square of every element. In $A_{4}$ the squares of the eight 3-cycles are again the eight 3-cycles (since $(a\;b\;c)^{2} = (a\;c\;b)$), too many for a group of order $6$.

Lagrange: for finite $G$, the order of every subgroup divides $|G|$, and there are $[G : H] = |G|/|H|$ cosets. The converse fails.

blocks.html: Lagrange's theorem is about subgroups, but its sharpest consequences are about single elements, because every element $a$ comes with its own subgroup $\langle a \rangle$, of order $|a|$.

Corollary 1. In a finite group, the order of every element divides $|G|$. Proof: $|a| = |\langle a \rangle|$, and $\langle a \rangle \le G$.
Corollary 2. $a^{|G|} = e$ for every $a \in G$. Proof: $|G| = |a|\,m$ for some $m$, so $a^{|G|} = (a^{|a|})^{m} = e$.
Corollary 3. A group of prime order $p$ is cyclic, and every element other than $e$ generates it. Proof: if $a \ne e$, then $|a|$ divides $p$ and is not $1$, so $|a| = p$ and $\langle a \rangle$ is all of $G$. $\square$

Fermat and Euler, again. Apply Corollary 2 to the group $U(n)$, of order $\varphi(n)$: for $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, $$a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod{n}.$$ This is Euler's theorem, and with $n = p$ prime it is Fermat's little theorem. The group-theory proof replaces a clever rearrangement argument by one line.

steps: So the subgroups are $\{e\}$ and $G$, and $G \cong \mathbb{Z}_{13}$ is cyclic, generated by any of its $12$ elements other than $e$.

blocks.html: These corollaries are why prime order is so restrictive: up to renaming, there is exactly one group of each prime order, the cyclic group. They also sort small groups quickly. In a group of order $4$, element orders divide $4$: either some element has order $4$ and the group is cyclic, or every element other than $e$ has order $2$. So there are just two kinds of group of order $4$, like $\mathbb{Z}_{4}$ and like $U(8)$.

Concluding that a group has an element of every order dividing $|G|$. $U(8) = \{1, 3, 5, 7\}$ has order $4$, but $3^{2} = 9 \equiv 1$, $5^{2} = 25 \equiv 1$, $7^{2} = 49 \equiv 1$: no element of order $4$. Lagrange limits element orders; it does not promise them.
In a finite group, $|a|$ divides $|G|$ and $a^{|G|} = e$. Groups of prime order are cyclic. In $U(n)$ this gives Euler's theorem, $a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod n$.

blocks.html: In the cosets lesson we saw that left and right cosets can differ. The subgroups for which they never differ are special: they are exactly the ones we can "divide by" to build a quotient group.

Definition. A subgroup $N$ of $G$ is normal, written $N \vartriangleleft G$ in many books, if $$gNg^{-1} = N \quad \text{for every } g \in G,$$ where $gNg^{-1} = \{gng^{-1} : n \in N\}$. Equivalent forms: $gN = Ng$ for every $g$; or, the test used in practice, $gng^{-1} \in N$ for every $g \in G$ and $n \in N$.

The element $gng^{-1}$ is a conjugate of $n$. Conjugating is "relabeling": in $S_{n}$, $\sigma\tau\sigma^{-1}$ is $\tau$ with every entry $i$ renamed $\sigma(i)$. So normal subgroups are the ones that look the same however you relabel the group.

Three families of normal subgroups.
(1) Every subgroup of an abelian group: $gng^{-1} = ngg^{-1} = n$.
(2) Every subgroup of index 2. There are only two left cosets, $N$ and $G \setminus N$, and only two right cosets, also $N$ and $G \setminus N$. So for $g \in N$, $gN = N = Ng$, and for $g \notin N$, $gN = G \setminus N = Ng$.
(3) The center $Z(G) = \{z : zg = gz \text{ for all } g\}$, since $gzg^{-1} = z$. $\square$

blocks.html: Arithmetic mod $n$ is arithmetic with cosets of $n\mathbb{Z}$: we add classes by adding any representatives. The same works in any group, provided the subgroup is normal.

Theorem. If $N$ is normal in $G$, the rule $(aN)(bN) = abN$ is well defined, and with it the set $G/N$ of cosets is a group, the quotient group (or factor group). Its identity is $eN = N$, the inverse of $aN$ is $a^{-1}N$, and $|G/N| = |G|/|N|$.
Proof of well-definedness. Suppose $aN = a'N$ and $bN = b'N$, so $a' = an_{1}$ and $b' = bn_{2}$ with $n_{1}, n_{2} \in N$. Then $$a'b' = a\,n_{1}\,b\,n_{2} = ab\,(b^{-1}n_{1}b)\,n_{2}.$$ Since $N$ is normal, $b^{-1}n_{1}b \in N$, so $a'b' \in abN$ and $a'b'N = abN$. The group axioms are inherited from $G$: $(aN)(bN)(cN) = abcN$ either way, $(eN)(aN) = aN$, and $(a^{-1}N)(aN) = N$. $\square$

Normality is exactly what makes this work. In $S_{3}$ with $H = \{e, (1\;2)\}$, the cosets $(1\;3)H$ and $(1\;3)(1\;2)H$ are equal, yet multiplying each by $(1\;3)H$ "by representatives" gives two different cosets. With a non-normal subgroup there is no quotient group.

blocks.html: A homomorphism is a map between groups that respects the operations. You know several already: $\det$ turns matrix products into number products, $e^{x}$ turns sums into products, and the sign of a permutation turns composition into multiplication of $\pm 1$. Like linear maps between vector spaces, homomorphisms let us compare groups.

Definition. A map $\varphi: G \to H$ between groups is a homomorphism if $$\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b) \quad \text{for all } a, b \in G,$$ where the product on the left is taken in $G$ and on the right in $H$. For example $\varphi: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}_{n}$, $x \mapsto x \bmod n$, and $\exp: (\mathbb{R}, +) \to (\mathbb{R}^{+}, \cdot)$, where the rule reads $e^{a + b} = e^{a}e^{b}$.

Basic properties. For a homomorphism $\varphi$:
(1) $\varphi(e_{G}) = e_{H}$: $\varphi(e) = \varphi(ee) = \varphi(e)\varphi(e)$, and cancelling $\varphi(e)$ gives $e_{H} = \varphi(e)$.
(2) $\varphi(a^{-1}) = \varphi(a)^{-1}$: $\varphi(a)\varphi(a^{-1}) = \varphi(aa^{-1}) = \varphi(e) = e$, and inverses are unique.
(3) $\varphi(a^{n}) = \varphi(a)^{n}$ for every integer $n$ (induction, with (2) for negatives).
(4) If $|a| = n$, then $|\varphi(a)|$ divides $n$: $\varphi(a)^{n} = \varphi(a^{n}) = \varphi(e) = e$. $\square$

blocks.html: If $G = \langle a \rangle$, then $\varphi(a^{k}) = \varphi(a)^{k}$, so $\varphi$ is decided by the single element $\varphi(a)$. For $\varphi: \mathbb{Z}_{m} \to \mathbb{Z}_{n}$ with $\varphi(1) = k$, the formula $\varphi(x) = kx \bmod n$ is well defined exactly when $mk \equiv 0 \pmod{n}$ (the elements $0$ and $m$ of $\mathbb{Z}$ are the same in $\mathbb{Z}_{m}$, so they must have the same image). Counting the solutions $k$ shows there are exactly $\gcd(m, n)$ homomorphisms $\mathbb{Z}_{m} \to \mathbb{Z}_{n}$.

So each of the $6$ elements works: $6$ homomorphisms. Only the two choices of a 3-cycle give an image of size $3$; none is onto, since $S_{3}$ is not cyclic.

$\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)$, using each group's own operation. Then $\varphi(e) = e$, $\varphi(a^{-1}) = \varphi(a)^{-1}$, $|\varphi(a)|$ divides $|a|$, and out of a cyclic group $\varphi$ is fixed by the image of a generator.

blocks.html: Every homomorphism comes with two subgroups: what it kills and what it reaches.
Definitions. For $\varphi: G \to H$, the kernel is $\ker\varphi = \{g \in G : \varphi(g) = e_{H}\}$ and the image is $\operatorname{im}\varphi = \{\varphi(g) : g \in G\}$.

Theorem. (1) $\operatorname{im}\varphi \le H$. (2) $\ker\varphi$ is a normal subgroup of $G$. (3) $\varphi(a) = \varphi(b)$ exactly when $a^{-1}b \in \ker\varphi$; so $\varphi$ is one-to-one exactly when $\ker\varphi = \{e\}$. (4) If $G$ is finite, $|G| = |\ker\varphi| \cdot |\operatorname{im}\varphi|$.
Proofs. (1) $\varphi(a)\varphi(b)^{-1} = \varphi(ab^{-1})$ lies in the image. (2) If $\varphi(a) = \varphi(b) = e$, then $\varphi(ab^{-1}) = e$, so the kernel is a subgroup; and for any $g$, $\varphi(gag^{-1}) = \varphi(g)\,e\,\varphi(g)^{-1} = e$, so it is normal. (3) $\varphi(a) = \varphi(b) \iff \varphi(a)^{-1}\varphi(b) = e \iff \varphi(a^{-1}b) = e$. (4) By (3), the elements sent to $\varphi(a)$ form the coset $a\ker\varphi$; the cosets of the kernel match the points of the image one for one, so $[G : \ker\varphi] = |\operatorname{im}\varphi|$. $\square$

blocks.html: Part (2) is also the fastest way to prove that a subgroup is normal: show that it is the kernel of some homomorphism. That is how we know at once that $A_{n}$ is normal in $S_{n}$, that $SL_{n}(\mathbb{R})$ is normal in $GL_{n}(\mathbb{R})$, and that $n\mathbb{Z}$ is normal in $\mathbb{Z}$, without conjugating a single element. Part (3) is the standard way to prove a homomorphism is one-to-one: compute the kernel instead of comparing pairs of elements.

Collecting the elements sent to the wrong identity. The kernel is everything sent to the identity of the target: that is $0$ for $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ but $1$ for $\mathbb{R}^{*}$ or $\{\pm 1\}$. And the kernel always contains $e$ (by $\varphi(e) = e$), so it is never empty; "one-to-one" means it contains nothing else.

A shortcut for normality. To prove a subgroup is normal, it is often quickest to show it is a kernel. $A_{n}$ is normal in $S_{n}$ because it is the kernel of the sign map, and $SL_{n}(\mathbb{R})$ is normal in $GL_{n}(\mathbb{R})$ because it is the kernel of $\det$.

$\ker\varphi$ (everything sent to $e$) is a normal subgroup;
 $\operatorname{im}\varphi$ is a subgroup; $\varphi$ is one-to-one iff the kernel is $\{e\}$; and $|G| = |\ker\varphi|\,|\operatorname{im}\varphi|$.

blocks.html: Two groups can look different on paper and be the same group in disguise: $U(10)$ and $\mathbb{Z}_{4}$ have the same multiplication pattern once you rename the elements. An isomorphism is such a renaming.

Definition. An isomorphism is a homomorphism that is a bijection. If one exists, $G$ and $H$ are isomorphic, $G \cong H$. The inverse of an isomorphism is again a homomorphism, so $\cong$ is an equivalence relation. By the kernel test, a homomorphism is one-to-one exactly when its kernel is trivial.
Write down a map and check the two conditions: it is a homomorphism, and it is a bijection (for finite groups of the same order, one-to-one is enough, and that is the kernel test).

Theorem. Every cyclic group of order $n$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$.
Proof. Let $G = \langle a \rangle$ with $|a| = n$, and define $\psi: \mathbb{Z}_{n} \to G$ by $\psi(k) = a^{k}$. It is well defined, because $a^{k} = a^{j}$ exactly when $k \equiv j \pmod n$ (the order lemma). It is a homomorphism: $\psi(j + k) = a^{j+k} = a^{j}a^{k}$. Its kernel is $\{k : a^{k} = e\} = \{0\}$, so it is one-to-one, and since both groups have $n$ elements it is onto. $\square$ The same argument shows every infinite cyclic group is $\cong \mathbb{Z}$.

blocks.html: Permutation groups are not just one example among many: every group is one, after an isomorphism. This is Cayley's theorem, and it is the reason permutations are a universal model for symmetry.

Cayley's theorem. Every group $G$ is isomorphic to a group of permutations of the set $G$. In particular a group of order $n$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $S_{n}$.
Proof. For $g \in G$ define $\lambda_{g}: G \to G$ by $\lambda_{g}(x) = gx$.
(1) $\lambda_{g}$ is a permutation: it has the inverse $\lambda_{g^{-1}}$, since $g^{-1}(gx) = x$.
(2) $g \mapsto \lambda_{g}$ is a homomorphism: $\lambda_{gh}(x) = ghx = \lambda_{g}(\lambda_{h}(x))$, so $\lambda_{gh} = \lambda_{g} \circ \lambda_{h}$.
(3) It is one-to-one: if $\lambda_{g}$ is the identity, then $g = ge = \lambda_{g}(e) = e$, so the kernel is trivial.
So $G \cong \{\lambda_{g} : g \in G\}$, a subgroup of the permutations of $G$. $\square$
You have already seen these permutations: $\lambda_{g}$ is row $g$ of the Cayley table, read as a rearrangement of the column headings. That every row is a rearrangement was the cancellation law.

blocks.html: Cayley's theorem is about existence, not economy: it puts a group of order $6$ inside $S_{6}$, which has $720$ elements, although $S_{3}$ is already a group of order $6$. Its value is conceptual. Any statement proved for all subgroups of symmetric groups holds for all finite groups, and any finite group can be explored by computer as a set of permutations.

Using $x \mapsto xg$ instead of $x \mapsto gx$. Right multiplication also permutes $G$, but $\rho_{g}(x) = xg$ gives $\rho_{gh}(x) = xgh = \rho_{h}(\rho_{g}(x))$: the order reverses, so $g \mapsto \rho_{g}$ is not a homomorphism in a nonabelian group (it works with $x \mapsto xg^{-1}$). In an abelian group the two agree.

Cayley: $g \mapsto \lambda_{g}$, with $\lambda_{g}(x) = gx$, is an isomorphism from $G$ onto a group of permutations of $G$. Each $\lambda_{g}$ is a row of the Cayley table, made of $|G|/|g|$ cycles of length $|g|$.

blocks.html: A homomorphism collapses its kernel to the identity and keeps everything else apart. The first isomorphism theorem says that this collapse is exactly a quotient group.

First isomorphism theorem. If $\varphi: G \to H$ is a homomorphism with kernel $K$, then $$G/K \cong \operatorname{im}\varphi, \quad \text{by } gK \mapsto \varphi(g).$$ Proof. Call the map $\psi$. Well defined: if $gK = g'K$ then $g^{-1}g' \in K$, so $\varphi(g)^{-1}\varphi(g') = \varphi(g^{-1}g') = e$ and $\varphi(g) = \varphi(g')$. Homomorphism: $\psi(gK\,g'K) = \psi(gg'K) = \varphi(gg') = \varphi(g)\varphi(g')$. One-to-one: $\psi(gK) = e$ means $g \in K$, so $gK = K$, the identity of $G/K$. Onto $\operatorname{im}\varphi$: every $\varphi(g)$ is $\psi(gK)$. $\square$

The theorem is a machine for naming quotients: to identify $G/N$, find a homomorphism out of $G$ whose kernel is $N$, and look at its image. It also explains the counting rule $|G| = |\ker\varphi|\,|\operatorname{im}\varphi|$.

blocks.html: The easiest way to build a new group from two old ones is to let them run side by side. This is also, as we will see, how every finite abelian group is built.

Definition. The direct product $G \times H$ is the set of pairs $(g, h)$ with the operation done coordinate by coordinate: $(g, h)(g', h') = (gg', hh')$. The identity is $(e, e)$, the inverse of $(g, h)$ is $(g^{-1}, h^{-1})$, and $|G \times H| = |G|\,|H|$. For additive groups we write $(a, b) + (a', b') = (a + a', b + b')$.

Order of a pair. $|(g, h)| = \operatorname{lcm}(|g|, |h|)$.
Proof. $(g, h)^{m} = (g^{m}, h^{m})$ is the identity exactly when $g^{m} = e$ and $h^{m} = e$, that is, when $|g| \mid m$ and $|h| \mid m$ (order lemma). The least such $m$ is the lcm. $\square$
Theorem. $\mathbb{Z}_{m} \times \mathbb{Z}_{n}$ is cyclic, and then $\cong \mathbb{Z}_{mn}$, exactly when $\gcd(m, n) = 1$.
Proof. Every element $(a, b)$ has order dividing $\operatorname{lcm}(m, n)$, and $(1, 1)$ has order exactly $\operatorname{lcm}(m, n)$. The group has $mn$ elements, so it is cyclic exactly when $\operatorname{lcm}(m, n) = mn$, that is, when $\gcd(m, n) = 1$; then $(1, 1)$ generates it, and every cyclic group of order $mn$ is $\cong \mathbb{Z}_{mn}$. $\square$ This is the Chinese remainder theorem in group language.

blocks.html: Many familiar groups are products in disguise. $U(8) \cong \mathbb{Z}_{2} \times \mathbb{Z}_{2}$ and $U(15) \cong \mathbb{Z}_{2} \times \mathbb{Z}_{4}$; in general, by the Chinese remainder theorem, $U(mn) \cong U(m) \times U(n)$ when $\gcd(m, n) = 1$.

Multiplying the orders instead of taking the lcm: in $\mathbb{Z}_{4} \times \mathbb{Z}_{6}$ the element $(1, 1)$ has order $12$, not $24$. And "same size means same group": $\mathbb{Z}_{2} \times \mathbb{Z}_{2}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_{4}$ both have four elements, but every element of $\mathbb{Z}_{2} \times \mathbb{Z}_{2}$ has order at most $2$, so it is not cyclic.
$G \times H$ works coordinate by coordinate, with $|(g, h)| = \operatorname{lcm}(|g|, |h|)$. $\mathbb{Z}_{m} \times \mathbb{Z}_{n} \cong \mathbb{Z}_{mn}$ exactly when $\gcd(m, n) = 1$.

blocks.html: Finite abelian groups can be listed completely: each one is a direct product of cyclic groups, in an essentially unique way. This is one of the great classification results of algebra, and it turns "how many abelian groups of order 72 are there?" into a counting exercise.

Fundamental theorem of finite abelian groups. Every finite abelian group is isomorphic to a product $$\mathbb{Z}_{p_{1}^{a_{1}}} \times \mathbb{Z}_{p_{2}^{a_{2}}} \times \cdots \times \mathbb{Z}_{p_{k}^{a_{k}}}$$ of cyclic groups of prime-power order (the primes need not be different). The list of prime powers, the elementary divisors, is unique up to order.

Why prime powers, and why partitions? Two facts from the last lesson do most of the work. First, $\mathbb{Z}_{mn} \cong \mathbb{Z}_{m} \times \mathbb{Z}_{n}$ for coprime $m, n$, so any cyclic factor splits into prime-power pieces, and pieces for different primes never interact. Second, for one prime $p$, products like $\mathbb{Z}_{p^{2}} \times \mathbb{Z}_{p}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_{p^{3}}$ are not isomorphic (count the elements of order $p$). So for a group of order $p^{a}$ the possible shapes match the ways to write $a = a_{1} + a_{2} + \cdots$ with $a_{1} \ge a_{2} \ge \cdots$: the partitions of $a$. The existence part of the theorem (that every abelian group splits this way) takes a longer argument; Judson proves it in chapter 13.

Counting. If $n = p_{1}^{e_{1}} \cdots p_{r}^{e_{r}}$, choose a partition of each exponent independently: the number of abelian groups of order $n$ is $\mathrm{p}(e_{1}) \cdots \mathrm{p}(e_{r})$, where $\mathrm{p}(e)$ is the number of partitions of $e$ ($\mathrm{p}(1) = 1$, $\mathrm{p}(2) = 2$, $\mathrm{p}(3) = 3$, $\mathrm{p}(4) = 5$, $\mathrm{p}(5) = 7$).

Always break factors into prime powers before comparing.

Every finite abelian group is a product of cyclic groups of prime-power order, uniquely. For order $p^{a}$ the groups match the partitions of $a$; for general $n$, multiply the partition counts of the exponents.

blocks.html: There is a second standard way to write a finite abelian group: with as few cyclic factors as possible, each order dividing the next. It answers questions like "what is the largest order of an element?" at a glance.

Invariant factor form. Every finite abelian group is isomorphic to exactly one $$\mathbb{Z}_{d_{1}} \times \mathbb{Z}_{d_{2}} \times \cdots \times \mathbb{Z}_{d_{k}} \quad \text{with } d_{1} \mid d_{2} \mid \cdots \mid d_{k},\ d_{1} \gt 1.$$ The $d_{i}$ are the invariant factors; $d_{k}$ is the largest order of an element (the exponent).

From elementary divisors to invariant factors. Write the prime powers for each prime in a row, largest first. Then $d_{k}$ is the product of the first entries of all rows, $d_{k-1}$ the product of the second entries, and so on. Each product uses coprime prime powers, so it is one cyclic group ($\mathbb{Z}_{m} \times \mathbb{Z}_{n} \cong \mathbb{Z}_{mn}$ for coprime $m, n$), and each $d_{i}$ divides the next because every row is in decreasing order. Going back is just factoring each $d_{i}$.

blocks.html: In $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ the equation $dx = 0$ has exactly $\gcd(d, n)$ solutions. In a product the solutions multiply, so the number of elements with order dividing $d$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{n_{1}} \times \cdots \times \mathbb{Z}_{n_{k}}$ is $\gcd(d, n_{1})\cdots\gcd(d, n_{k})$. Subtract the counts for proper divisors of $d$ to get the elements of order exactly $d$.

blocks.html: Merging factors whose orders share a prime: $\mathbb{Z}_{2} \times \mathbb{Z}_{4}$ is not $\mathbb{Z}_{8}$ (it has no element of order 8). Only coprime orders combine. In the row method this is automatic: a column never contains two powers of the same prime.

Telling groups apart. $\mathbb{Z}_{6} \times \mathbb{Z}_{12}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_{2} \times \mathbb{Z}_{36}$ both have order $72$, and both are already in invariant factor form. The lists $(6, 12)$ and $(2, 36)$ differ, so the groups are not isomorphic. A direct witness: $\mathbb{Z}_{2} \times \mathbb{Z}_{36}$ has an element of order $36$, while every element of $\mathbb{Z}_{6} \times \mathbb{Z}_{12}$ has order dividing $12$.

 built from the elementary divisors column by column. Two finite abelian groups are isomorphic exactly when their invariant factors match.

blocks.html: Groups earn their keep by moving things: symmetries move the corners of a polygon, permutations move numbers, matrices move vectors. A group action makes "moving things" precise, and it turns many counting problems into group theory.

Definition. A group $G$ acts on a set $X$ if each $g \in G$ and $x \in X$ give a point $g \cdot x \in X$, with $$e \cdot x = x \quad \text{and} \quad g \cdot (h \cdot x) = (gh) \cdot x.$$ Equivalently, each $g$ gives a permutation of $X$, and $g \mapsto$ (that permutation) is a homomorphism from $G$ to the permutations of $X$.

items: $S_{n}$ acts on $\{1, \dots, n\}$ by $\sigma \cdot i = \sigma(i)$.
$D_{n}$ acts on the vertices, and on the edges, of a regular $n$-gon.
$GL_{2}(\mathbb{R})$ acts on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ by $A \cdot v = Av$.
$G$ acts on itself by left multiplication, $g \cdot x = gx$ (Cayley's theorem), and by conjugation, $g \cdot x = gxg^{-1}$.

blocks.html: Orbits and stabilizers. The orbit of $x$ is $G \cdot x = \{g \cdot x : g \in G\}$, everywhere $x$ can be moved. The stabilizer of $x$ is $G_{x} = \{g \in G : g \cdot x = x\}$, the elements that leave it in place.

(1) The orbits split $X$ into disjoint pieces. Say $x \sim y$ when $y = g \cdot x$ for some $g$. This is an equivalence relation: $x = e \cdot x$; if $y = g \cdot x$ then $x = g^{-1} \cdot y$ (apply $g^{-1}$ and use the rule); if $y = g \cdot x$ and $z = h \cdot y$ then $z = (hg) \cdot x$. Its classes are the orbits.
(2) Each stabilizer is a subgroup. $e \cdot x = x$; if $g, h$ fix $x$ then $(gh) \cdot x = g \cdot (h \cdot x) = x$, and $g^{-1} \cdot x = g^{-1} \cdot (g \cdot x) = e \cdot x = x$. $\square$

blocks.q: $S_{4}$ acts on the 2-element subsets of $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$. Find the stabilizer of $\{1, 2\}$.
steps: $\sigma$ fixes the set $\{1, 2\}$ when it sends $\{1, 2\}$ to itself, and hence $\{3, 4\}$ to itself.

blocks.html: Counting a point twice. The orbit is a set: if two group elements send $x$ to the same place, that place is counted once. Its size is usually smaller than $|G|$. The reverse slip is assuming the stabilizer is always $\{e\}$: for a vertex of a polygon it also contains the reflection through that vertex.
An action lets each $g$ move points, with $e \cdot x = x$ and $g \cdot (h \cdot x) = (gh) \cdot x$. Orbits (where a point can go) partition the set; stabilizers (what fixes a point) are subgroups.

blocks.html: How many rotations does a cube have? Counting them one by one is error-prone. The orbit–stabilizer theorem gets the answer from two easy counts, by the same partition idea that proved Lagrange's theorem.

Orbit–stabilizer theorem. If a finite group $G$ acts on $X$ and $x \in X$, then $$|G \cdot x| = [G : G_{x}], \qquad \text{so} \qquad |G| = |G \cdot x| \cdot |G_{x}|.$$ Proof. Match each left coset of the stabilizer with a point of the orbit by $gG_{x} \mapsto g \cdot x$.
Well defined and one-to-one: $g \cdot x = h \cdot x \iff (h^{-1}g) \cdot x = x \iff h^{-1}g \in G_{x} \iff gG_{x} = hG_{x}$ (reading the chain left to right gives one-to-one, right to left gives well defined).
Onto: every point of the orbit is some $g \cdot x$.
So the number of cosets, $[G : G_{x}] = |G|/|G_{x}|$, equals the size of the orbit. $\square$
So orbit sizes always divide $|G|$. If any two of $|G|$, the orbit size and the stabilizer size are known, so is the third.

blocks.title: The rotations of a cube
blocks.q: How many rotations does a cube have?
steps: Act on the $6$ faces: any face can be rotated to any other, so the orbit of the top face has $6$ elements.
Rotations fixing the top face spin about the vertical axis: $0^\circ$, $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$, $270^\circ$. The stabilizer has $4$ elements.
$|G| = 6 \cdot 4 = 24$. Check with vertices: $8$ vertices, $3$ rotations fix a given vertex, $8 \cdot 3 = 24$.

blocks.title: Subsets
blocks.q: $S_{6}$ acts on the 2-element subsets of $\{1, \dots, 6\}$. Use orbit–stabilizer to count them.
steps: Every 2-subset can be moved to every other, so there is one orbit: all of them.
The stabilizer of $\{1, 2\}$ permutes $\{1, 2\}$ and $\{3, 4, 5, 6\}$ separately: $2! \cdot 4! = 48$ elements.

blocks.title: Conjugacy classes in $S_{4}$
blocks.q: $(1\;2)$ commutes with exactly $4$ permutations of $S_{4}$. How many permutations are conjugate to it?
steps: Let $S_{4}$ act on itself by conjugation; the stabilizer of $(1\;2)$ is the set of permutations commuting with it, of size $4$.

blocks.html: Multiplying when you should divide, or using the size of the whole set in place of the orbit. For the cube acting on its $8$ vertices, the stabilizer of a vertex has $24/8 = 3$ elements only because the vertices form a single orbit; when there are several orbits, use the size of the orbit of that point.
For a finite group acting on a set: $|G| = |\text{orbit of } x| \cdot |\text{stabilizer of } x|$. The points of the orbit match the cosets of the stabilizer.

blocks.html: Let a group act on itself by conjugation, $g \cdot x = gxg^{-1}$. The orbits are called conjugacy classes, and counting them gives an equation with real consequences for groups of prime-power order.

Definitions. The conjugacy class of $x$ is $\{gxg^{-1} : g \in G\}$. The stabilizer of $x$ is its centralizer $C(x) = \{g : gx = xg\}$. The class of $x$ is $\{x\}$ alone exactly when $x$ commutes with everything, that is, when $x$ is in the center $Z(G)$.

The class equation. The classes partition $G$. Collect the one-element classes (the center) and pick one $x_{i}$ from each larger class; by orbit–stabilizer each class has $[G : C(x_{i})]$ elements, so $$|G| = |Z(G)| + \sum_{i} [G : C(x_{i})],$$ and every term divides $|G|$.
Application. If $|G| = p^{n}$ with $p$ prime and $n \ge 1$, then $Z(G) \ne \{e\}$. Proof: each $[G : C(x_{i})]$ is a divisor of $p^{n}$ bigger than $1$, so a multiple of $p$. Then $|Z(G)| = |G| - \sum [G : C(x_{i})]$ is a multiple of $p$, and it is at least $1$ (it contains $e$), so it is at least $p$. $\square$

Classes in $S_{n}$. Conjugating relabels: $\sigma(a_{1}\;\dots\;a_{k})\sigma^{-1} = (\sigma(a_{1})\;\dots\;\sigma(a_{k}))$. So two permutations are conjugate exactly when they have the same cycle type, and the classes of $S_{n}$ match the partitions of $n$.
