blocks.html: Counting the central elements twice: they appear as the term $|Z(G)|$, so the sum runs only over classes with more than one element. A quick check on any class equation: every term divides $|G|$, and the terms add up to $|G|$. For $D_{4}$, $1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8$.

One more step: groups of order $p^{2}$ are abelian. Suppose $|G| = p^{2}$ and $Z(G) \ne G$. Then $|Z(G)| = p$. Pick $x \notin Z(G)$: its centralizer $C(x)$ contains all of $Z(G)$ and also $x$, so $|C(x)| \gt p$, and by Lagrange $C(x) = G$. That says $x$ commutes with everything, so $x \in Z(G)$, a contradiction. $\square$

Conjugacy classes are the orbits of conjugation; the class of $x$ has $[G : C(x)]$ elements. $|G| = |Z(G)| + \sum [G : C(x_{i})]$. In $S_{n}$ the classes are the cycle types; groups of order $p^{n}$ have a nontrivial center.

blocks.html: How many different necklaces can you make with 6 beads in 2 colors, if turning a necklace does not change it? There are $2^{6} = 64$ colorings, and the rotations group them into orbits; the question asks for the number of orbits. Dividing by the number of rotations fails, because orbits have different sizes. Burnside's lemma counts them correctly.

Burnside's lemma. If a finite group $G$ acts on a finite set $X$, the number of orbits is $$\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} |\mathrm{Fix}(g)|, \qquad \mathrm{Fix}(g) = \{x : g \cdot x = x\}.$$ Proof. Count the pairs $(g, x)$ with $g \cdot x = x$ in two ways. By $g$: $\sum_{g} |\mathrm{Fix}(g)|$. By $x$: $\sum_{x} |G_{x}|$, and by orbit–stabilizer $|G_{x}| = |G|/|G \cdot x|$. So $$\sum_{g} |\mathrm{Fix}(g)| = |G| \sum_{x} \frac{1}{|G \cdot x|}.$$ The points of one orbit $O$ contribute $|O| \cdot \frac{1}{|O|} = 1$, so the last sum is the number of orbits. $\square$

Counting fixed colorings. A coloring is fixed by a symmetry exactly when the symmetry never moves a bead onto a bead of a different color, that is, when each cycle of the symmetry (as a permutation of the beads) is a single color. With $k$ colors and $c$ cycles, $k^{c}$ colorings are fixed. Rotating $n$ beads by $j$ steps has $\gcd(n, j)$ cycles.

That shortcut assumes every orbit has $|G|$ members, which fails whenever some coloring is fixed by a symmetry other than $e$ (the one-color necklaces are fixed by everything). Burnside's average of fixed counts is always a whole number; if yours is not, recount the cycles.

blocks.html: Lagrange's theorem says which subgroup orders are possible but promises none, and its converse fails. For prime powers, though, there is a strong partial converse. The Sylow theorems, proved with group actions, are the main tool for understanding groups of a given order.
Write $|G| = p^{a}m$ with $p$ prime and $p \nmid m$. A subgroup of order $p^{a}$, the largest power of $p$ dividing $|G|$, is a Sylow $p$-subgroup.

items: Sylow I (existence). $G$ has a Sylow $p$-subgroup. (Hence, by Cauchy's theorem, $G$ has an element of order $p$ for every prime $p$ dividing $|G|$.)
Sylow II (conjugacy). Any two Sylow $p$-subgroups are conjugate: $Q = gPg^{-1}$ for some $g$.
Sylow III (counting). The number $n_{p}$ of Sylow $p$-subgroups satisfies $n_{p} \mid m$ and $n_{p} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$.

blocks.html: Why $n_{p} = 1$ means normal. A conjugate $gPg^{-1}$ of a Sylow $p$-subgroup is again a subgroup of order $p^{a}$, so it is a Sylow $p$-subgroup. If there is only one, every conjugate of $P$ is $P$: $P$ is normal. Conversely, if $P$ is normal, Sylow II says every Sylow $p$-subgroup is a conjugate of $P$, hence $P$. (The proofs of the three theorems use group actions on subsets and the class equation; see Judson, chapter 15.)

blocks.title: Order 20
blocks.q: Must a group of order $20$ have a normal subgroup of order $5$?
steps: So $n_{5} = 1$, and the Sylow 5-subgroup is normal.

blocks.title: Order 15 is cyclic
blocks.q: Show that every group of order $15$ is cyclic.
steps: So there is one subgroup $P$ of order 3 and one, $Q$, of order 5; they hold $2 + 4 = 6$ non-identity elements.
The other $15 - 1 - 6 = 8$ elements have order dividing $15$ but not $1$, $3$ or $5$: order $15$. So the group is cyclic.

blocks.title: Order 12
blocks.q: What are the possible values of $n_{3}$ for a group of order $12$?
steps: Candidates $1, 2, 4$: $n_{3} \in \{1, 4\}$. Both happen: $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ has $n_{3} = 1$, and $A_{4}$ has $n_{3} = 4$ (the subgroups generated by its eight 3-cycles, two per subgroup).

blocks.html: Counting elements is a frequent finishing move: Sylow subgroups of prime order $p$ meet only in $e$, so $n_{p}$ of them hold $n_{p}(p - 1)$ elements of order $p$. If these counts add up to more than $|G|$, some $n_{p}$ must be $1$.

Using $n_{p} \mid |G|$ instead of $n_{p} \mid m$, or forgetting $n_{p} \equiv 1 \pmod p$. For $|G| = 20$, "$n_{5}$ divides $20$" would allow $n_{5} = 4$ or $10$; the correct conditions force $n_{5} = 1$. And remember what $n_{p} = 1$ buys you: a normal Sylow $p$-subgroup.

If $|G| = p^{a}m$ with $p \nmid m$, Sylow subgroups of order $p^{a}$ exist and are all conjugate, and their number satisfies $n_{p} \mid m$ and $n_{p} \equiv 1 \pmod p$; $n_{p} = 1$ exactly when the Sylow $p$-subgroup is normal.

blocks.html: Integers, matrices, polynomials and residues mod n can all be added and multiplied. A ring is the structure with both operations, linked by the distributive law. Everything you learned about groups applies to the addition.
Definition. A ring is a set $R$ with two operations, $+$ and $\cdot$, such that

items: $(R, +)$ is an abelian group (identity $0$, inverses $-a$);
multiplication is associative: $(ab)c = a(bc)$;
multiplication distributes over addition: $a(b + c) = ab + ac$ and $(a + b)c = ac + bc$.

blocks.html: A ring is commutative if $ab = ba$ always, and has an identity (or unity) if some $1 \ne 0$ has $1a = a1 = a$. A unit is an element with a multiplicative inverse; the units form a group $U(R)$ under multiplication. Examples: $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ (units $U(n)$), polynomials $\mathbb{R}[x]$, the $2 \times 2$ real matrices (not commutative; units are the invertible matrices), and $2\mathbb{Z}$ (no identity).

Rules that follow from the axioms. In any ring, $0a = 0$ and $(-a)b = -(ab)$.
Proof. $0a = (0 + 0)a = 0a + 0a$ by distributivity; adding $-(0a)$ to both sides gives $0 = 0a$. Next, $ab + (-a)b = (a + (-a))b = 0b = 0$, so $(-a)b$ is the additive inverse of $ab$. $\square$ So "a negative times a positive is negative" is not a convention: it is forced by distributivity. Applying the second rule twice gives $(-a)(-b) = ab$.

blocks.cap: The multiplication table of the ring $\mathbb{Z}_{6}$. The units $1$ and $5$ have a $1$ in their rows; $2 \cdot 3 = 0$ although neither factor is $0$.

blocks.title: Units of a product ring
blocks.q: How many units does $\mathbb{Z}_{4} \times \mathbb{Z}_{9}$ have (operations coordinate by coordinate)?
steps: $(a, b)$ has an inverse exactly when $a$ is a unit of $\mathbb{Z}_{4}$ and $b$ is a unit of $\mathbb{Z}_{9}$.

blocks.title: Matrices over $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ do not commute
blocks.q: In the ring of $2 \times 2$ matrices over $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$, compare $AB$ and $BA$ for $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

blocks.html: The characteristic of a ring with identity is the least $n \ge 1$ with $n \cdot 1 = 1 + \cdots + 1 = 0$, or $0$ if there is none: $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ has characteristic $n$, $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ have characteristic $0$, and $\mathbb{Z}_{4} \times \mathbb{Z}_{6}$ has characteristic $\operatorname{lcm}(4, 6) = 12$.

Assuming a ring's multiplication commutes, or that a ring has a $1$. Matrix rings fail the first ($AB \ne BA$ above), and $2\mathbb{Z}$ fails the second: no even number $u$ has $u \cdot 2 = 2$. Many statements about "rings" in this course say "commutative ring with identity" for exactly this reason.
A ring is an abelian group under $+$ with an associative, distributive multiplication. Units are the invertible elements. From the axioms, $0a = 0$ and $(-a)b = -(ab)$.

blocks.html: In $\mathbb{Z}$, if $ab = 0$ then $a = 0$ or $b = 0$; that is how you solve $(x - 2)(x - 3) = 0$. In other rings this can fail: $2 \cdot 3 = 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{6}$. The rings where it holds are the ones where algebra behaves the way you expect.

Definitions. In a commutative ring, $a e 0$ is a zero divisor if $ab = 0$ for some $b e 0$. An integral domain is a commutative ring with identity $1 e 0$ and no zero divisors. A field is a commutative ring with $1 e 0$ in which every nonzero element is a unit. Examples of fields: $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{C}$, $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$. Integral domains that are not fields: $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.

(1) Fields are integral domains. If $ab = 0$ and $a e 0$, multiply by $a^{-1}$: $b = a^{-1}ab = 0$.
(2) Cancellation. In an integral domain, $ab = ac$ with $a e 0$ gives $a(b - c) = 0$, so $b = c$.
(3) $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ is a field exactly when $n$ is prime. If $n = rs$ with $1 \lt r, s \lt n$, then $rs = 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$: zero divisors. If $n = p$ is prime, every $a e 0$ has $\gcd(a, p) = 1$, so it is a unit.
(4) A finite integral domain is a field. For $a e 0$, the map $x \mapsto ax$ is one-to-one by cancellation, hence onto (the ring is finite), so $ax = 1$ for some $x$. $\square$

blocks.name: aa-cayley
blocks.cap: Multiplication in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$. Every zero inside the table (away from the row and column of $0$) is a pair of zero divisors; the rows of $1, 5, 7, 11$ contain a $1$ instead.

blocks.title: Zero divisors of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$
blocks.q: List the zero divisors of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$.
steps: $a \ne 0$ is a zero divisor exactly when $\gcd(a, 12) \gt 1$: then $a \cdot \frac{12}{\gcd(a, 12)} \equiv 0$.
blocks.a: $\{2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10\}$; the other nonzero elements are units.

blocks.title: Solving when you cannot cancel
blocks.q: Solve $4x = 8$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$, and $3x = 5$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{7}$.
steps: In $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$, $4$ is a zero divisor, so we cannot cancel. Testing: $x = 2, 5, 8, 11$ all give $4x \equiv 8$.

blocks.title: Products of rings
blocks.q: Is $\mathbb{Z}_{3} \times \mathbb{Z}_{5}$ an integral domain?
blocks.a: No, though each factor is a field.

blocks.html: Cancelling in $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ for composite $n$: from $2 \cdot 3 = 2 \cdot 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{6}$ you cannot conclude $3 = 0$. Cancellation needs an integral domain. A related slip: "$x^{2} = x$ means $x = 0$ or $1$" fails in $\mathbb{Z}_{6}$, where $3^{2} = 3$ and $4^{2} = 4$.

Zero divisors are nonzero $a, b$ with $ab = 0$. Integral domains have none, so cancellation works; fields have inverses for every nonzero element. $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ is a field exactly when $n$ is prime, and every finite integral domain is a field.

blocks.html: For groups, the subgroups you can divide by are the normal ones. For rings, they are the ideals: additive subgroups that swallow products with anything in the ring. The multiples of $n$ in $\mathbb{Z}$ are the model.

Definition. An ideal of a commutative ring $R$ is an additive subgroup $I$ such that $ra \in I$ for every $r \in R$ and $a \in I$. (In a noncommutative ring a two-sided ideal also needs $ar \in I$.) Ideal test: $I$ is nonempty, $a - b \in I$ and $ra \in I$ for all $a, b \in I$, $r \in R$.
Principal ideals. For $a \in R$ (commutative, with $1$), $(a) = \{ra : r \in R\}$ is the smallest ideal containing $a$. More generally $(a, b) = \{ra + sb : r, s \in R\}$.

Every ideal of $\mathbb{Z}$ is principal: $I = (n)$ for some $n \ge 0$.
Proof. If $I = \{0\}$, it is $(0)$. Otherwise $I$ contains a positive number (if $a \in I$ then $-a \in I$); let $n$ be the smallest. Then $(n) \subseteq I$. For $a \in I$ divide: $a = nq + r$ with $0 \le r \lt n$; then $r = a - qn \in I$, so $r = 0$ by the choice of $n$. Hence $I = (n)$. $\square$ This is the same argument that showed subgroups of cyclic groups are cyclic. Consequences in $\mathbb{Z}$: $(a, b) = (\gcd(a, b))$ (Bézout), $(a) \cap (b) = (\operatorname{lcm}(a, b))$ and $(a)(b) = (ab)$.

In $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$, every additive subgroup $\langle d \rangle$ is automatically an ideal ($r \cdot kd = (rk)d$ is again a multiple of $d$), so the ideals are $(d)$ for $d \mid n$, one for each divisor.

blocks.name: aa-lattice
blocks.cap: The six ideals of the ring $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$, one for each divisor of 12, ordered by inclusion.

blocks.title: Ideals of $\mathbb{Z}$
blocks.q: Write $(12, 18)$, $(4) \cap (6)$ and $(4) + (6)$ as principal ideals of $\mathbb{Z}$.

blocks.title: An ideal of $\mathbb{Z}[x]$
blocks.q: Is $I = \{f \in \mathbb{Z}[x] : f(0) \text{ is even}\}$ an ideal?
steps: $0 \in I$, and $(f - g)(0) = f(0) - g(0)$ is even when both are.
It is the ideal $(2, x)$: the polynomials $2a(x) + x\,b(x)$.

blocks.html: A field $F$ has only the ideals $\{0\}$ and $F$: an ideal containing $a \ne 0$ contains $a^{-1}a = 1$ and then every $r = r \cdot 1$.

Checking only products of two elements of $I$. An ideal must absorb products with every element of the ring. $\mathbb{Z}$ is closed under addition and multiplication inside $\mathbb{Q}$ (it is a subring), yet $\frac{1}{2} \cdot 1 \notin \mathbb{Z}$, so it is not an ideal of $\mathbb{Q}$.

An ideal is an additive subgroup that absorbs multiplication by any ring element. Every ideal of $\mathbb{Z}$ is $(n)$; $(a, b) = (\gcd)$, $(a) \cap (b) = (\operatorname{lcm})$; the ideals of $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ are $(d)$ for $d \mid n$.

blocks.html: A ring homomorphism is a group homomorphism for addition that also respects multiplication. Its kernel turns out to be an ideal, just as the kernel of a group homomorphism is a normal subgroup.

Definition. $\varphi: R \to S$ is a ring homomorphism if $$\varphi(a + b) = \varphi(a) + \varphi(b) \quad \text{and} \quad \varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)$$ for all $a, b$. Its kernel is $\ker\varphi = \{a : \varphi(a) = 0\}$.

The kernel is an ideal. It is an additive subgroup, being the kernel of the additive group homomorphism. And if $\varphi(a) = 0$ then $\varphi(ra) = \varphi(r)\varphi(a) = \varphi(r) \cdot 0 = 0$. $\square$ As for groups, $\varphi$ is one-to-one exactly when $\ker\varphi = \{0\}$.

items: Reduction $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}_{n}$, $a \mapsto a \bmod n$: kernel $(n)$. Also $\mathbb{Z}_{12} \to \mathbb{Z}_{4}$, since $4 \mid 12$.
Evaluation $\mathbb{R}[x] \to \mathbb{R}$, $f \mapsto f(c)$: kernel $\{f : f(c) = 0\} = (x - c)$, by the factor theorem.
Complex conjugation $\mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$: one-to-one and onto.
Not one: $x \mapsto 2x$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ keeps sums but $\varphi(1 \cdot 1) = 2 \ne 4 = \varphi(1)\varphi(1)$.

blocks.title: Evaluation
blocks.q: Find $\varphi(f)$ for $\varphi: \mathbb{Z}[x] \to \mathbb{Z}$, $f \mapsto f(-2)$, and $f = x^{3} - 3x + 1$. Describe the kernel.
steps: The kernel is the polynomials with root $-2$: the ideal $(x + 2)$.

blocks.title: Two moduli at once
blocks.q: Find the kernel of $\varphi: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}_{4} \times \mathbb{Z}_{6}$, $a \mapsto (a \bmod 4, a \bmod 6)$.
steps: $\varphi(a) = (0, 0)$ when $4 \mid a$ and $6 \mid a$, that is, $12 \mid a$.
So $\ker\varphi = (12)$. The image has $12$ elements, fewer than $24$, so $\varphi$ is not onto (the moduli share a factor).

blocks.title: Is it a ring homomorphism?
blocks.q: Is $\varphi: \mathbb{Z}_{6} \to \mathbb{Z}_{6}$, $\varphi(x) = 3x$, a ring homomorphism? What about $4x$?
steps: Both preserve sums. For products, $\varphi(xy) = kxy$ must equal $\varphi(x)\varphi(y) = k^{2}xy$, so we need $k^{2} \equiv k \pmod 6$.
blocks.a: Both are, since $3$ and $4$ satisfy $k^{2} = k$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{6}$.

blocks.html: A ring homomorphism out of $\mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ is decided by $e = \varphi(1)$, because $\varphi(k) = \varphi(1 + \cdots + 1) = ke$. The product rule then forces $e^{2} = \varphi(1 \cdot 1) = e$: the image of $1$ must be an idempotent. In a field or an integral domain the only idempotents are $0$ and $1$ (from $e(e - 1) = 0$), but rings like $\mathbb{Z}_{6}$ have more, which is why the last example found extra homomorphisms.

Checking only addition. $x \mapsto 2x$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ preserves every sum but fails on products, so it is a group homomorphism and not a ring homomorphism. When the map is determined by $\varphi(1) = e$, the product rule forces $e^{2} = e$: test that first.
A ring homomorphism preserves $+$ and $\cdot$; its kernel is an ideal, and it is one-to-one iff the kernel is $\{0\}$. Reduction mod $n$ and evaluation at a point are the key examples.

blocks.html: Arithmetic mod $n$ is arithmetic in a quotient ring: $\mathbb{Z}_{n} = \mathbb{Z}/(n)$. The same construction with any ideal produces new rings, including $\mathbb{C}$ out of real polynomials and the finite fields at the end of the course. It is the ring version of a quotient group.

Theorem. If $I$ is an ideal of a commutative ring $R$, the cosets $a + I$ form a ring $R/I$ with $$(a + I) + (b + I) = (a + b) + I, \qquad (a + I)(b + I) = ab + I.$$ Why multiplication is well defined. If $a' = a + i$ and $b' = b + j$ with $i, j \in I$, then $$a'b' = ab + aj + ib + ij,$$ and $aj$, $ib$, $ij$ all lie in $I$ because $I$ absorbs products. So $a'b' + I = ab + I$. (Addition is well defined because $I$ is a normal subgroup of the abelian group $(R, +)$.) The ring axioms carry over from $R$. $\square$

Computing in $F[x]/(f)$. Two polynomials name the same coset when they differ by a multiple of $f$, so every coset has exactly one representative of degree less than $\deg f$: the remainder after dividing by $f$. In practice, replace high powers of $x$ using $f = 0$. Over $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$, with $\deg f = n$, there are $p^{n}$ remainders, so $\mathbb{Z}_{p}[x]/(f)$ has $p^{n}$ elements.

blocks.title: Complex numbers from polynomials
blocks.q: In $\mathbb{R}[x]/(x^{2} + 1)$, compute $(2 + 3x)(1 - x)$.
steps: Compare $(2 + 3i)(1 - i) = 5 + i$: the class of $x$ behaves exactly like $i$, and $\mathbb{R}[x]/(x^{2} + 1) \cong \mathbb{C}$.

blocks.title: A quotient of $\mathbb{Z}_{2}[x]$
blocks.q: In $\mathbb{Z}_{2}[x]/(x^{2} + x + 1)$, list the elements and compute $x \cdot (x + 1)$.
steps: Remainders of degree less than $2$: $0, 1, x, x + 1$.
blocks.a: $x$ and $x + 1$ are inverses; this four-element ring is a field.

blocks.title: A finite quotient of $\mathbb{Z}$
blocks.q: In $\mathbb{Z}_{12}/(4)$, compute $(7 + I)(5 + I)$ with $I = (4)$.
steps: $7 \cdot 5 = 35$, and cosets of $(4)$ are classes mod $4$: $35 \equiv 3$.
blocks.a: $3 + I$; the ring is a copy of $\mathbb{Z}_{4}$.

blocks.html: The first isomorphism theorem holds for rings too: if $\varphi: R \to S$ is a ring homomorphism, then $R/\ker\varphi \cong \operatorname{im}\varphi$. For example, evaluation at $i$ sends $\mathbb{R}[x]$ onto $\mathbb{C}$ with kernel $(x^{2} + 1)$, which is another way to see $\mathbb{R}[x]/(x^{2} + 1) \cong \mathbb{C}$.

Reducing by the wrong polynomial, or forgetting the coefficients.
 In $\mathbb{Z}_{p}[x]/(f)$ there are two reductions: coefficients mod $p$, and powers of $x$ using $f = 0$. Check the final answer: its degree must be less than $\deg f$ and its coefficients between $0$ and $p - 1$.
For an ideal $I$, the cosets $a + I$ form the ring $R/I$. In $F[x]/(f)$ each element is a remainder of degree below $\deg f$; compute by multiplying and reducing with $f = 0$.

blocks.html: Which quotient rings are integral domains, and which are fields? The answer depends only on the ideal, and it is the bridge from polynomials to field extensions.

Definitions. In a commutative ring $R$ with identity, a proper ideal $P \ne R$ is prime if $ab \in P$ implies $a \in P$ or $b \in P$. A proper ideal $M$ is maximal if the only ideals containing $M$ are $M$ and $R$. In $\mathbb{Z}$, $(p)$ is prime exactly when $p$ is prime (this is "a prime dividing a product divides a factor"), and $(0)$ is prime too.

Theorem. (1) $R/P$ is an integral domain exactly when $P$ is prime. (2) $R/M$ is a field exactly when $M$ is maximal. So every maximal ideal is prime.
Proof of (1). $(a + P)(b + P) = 0 + P$ means $ab \in P$; "no zero divisors in $R/P$" says this forces $a \in P$ or $b \in P$, which is the definition of prime.
Proof of (2). Suppose $M$ is maximal and $a \notin M$. The ideal $M + (a) = \{m + ra\}$ is bigger than $M$, so it is $R$, and $1 = m + ra$ for some $m \in M$, $r \in R$. Then $(r + M)(a + M) = 1 + M$: every nonzero coset has an inverse. Conversely, if $R/M$ is a field and $J \supsetneq M$ is an ideal, pick $a \in J \setminus M$; then $a + M$ has an inverse $r + M$, so $1 - ra \in M \subseteq J$, hence $1 \in J$ and $J = R$. $\square$

blocks.html: In $F[x]$. Every ideal is $(f)$ for one polynomial (the division algorithm gives this, as for $\mathbb{Z}$), and $(f)$ is maximal exactly when $f$ is irreducible. So $F[x]/(f)$ is a field exactly when $f$ is irreducible: this is how we will build new fields.

blocks.cap: The ideals of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$. The maximal ones, $(2)$ and $(3)$, sit just below the whole ring; the quotients $\mathbb{Z}_{12}/(2) \cong \mathbb{Z}_{2}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_{12}/(3) \cong \mathbb{Z}_{3}$ are fields.

blocks.title: Maximal ideals of $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$
blocks.q: List the maximal ideals of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$.
steps: $\mathbb{Z}_{d}$ is a field exactly when $d$ is prime: $d = 2, 3$.

blocks.title: A polynomial ideal
blocks.q: Is $(x^{2} + 1)$ maximal in $\mathbb{Z}_{3}[x]$? In $\mathbb{Z}_{5}[x]$?
steps: Over $\mathbb{Z}_{3}$: $0^{2} + 1 = 1$, $1^{2} + 1 = 2$, $2^{2} + 1 = 5 \equiv 2$: no root, and a quadratic with no root is irreducible. Maximal.
Over $\mathbb{Z}_{5}$: $2^{2} + 1 = 5 \equiv 0$, so $x - 2$ divides it. Not maximal (not even prime).

blocks.html: Thinking every prime ideal is maximal. $(x)$ in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is prime, because $\mathbb{Z}[x]/(x) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ is an integral domain, but not maximal, because $\mathbb{Z}$ is not a field; indeed $(x) \subsetneq (2, x) \subsetneq \mathbb{Z}[x]$. (In a finite ring the two notions agree, since finite integral domains are fields.)
$P$ is prime iff $R/P$ is an integral domain; $M$ is maximal iff $R/M$ is a field; maximal implies prime. In $F[x]$, $(f)$ is maximal exactly when $f$ is irreducible.

blocks.html: You have multiplied polynomials with real coefficients for years. The same rules work with coefficients in any ring, and polynomials over $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ will build the finite fields. But the coefficient ring matters: over $\mathbb{Z}_{6}$ some familiar facts fail.

Definition. For a commutative ring $R$, $R[x]$ is the set of expressions $a_{n}x^{n} + \cdots + a_{1}x + a_{0}$ with $a_{i} \in R$, added and multiplied as usual, with the coefficients computed in $R$: $$\Big(\sum a_{i}x^{i}\Big)\Big(\sum b_{j}x^{j}\Big) = \sum_{k} \Big(\sum_{i + j = k} a_{i}b_{j}\Big)x^{k}.$$ The degree is the highest power with a nonzero coefficient, the leading coefficient. Over $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ we write coefficients from $0$ to $n - 1$.

Theorem. If $R$ is an integral domain, then $\deg(fg) = \deg f + \deg g$ for nonzero $f, g$, and $R[x]$ is an integral domain.
Proof. If $f$ has leading term $a_{m}x^{m}$ and $g$ has $b_{n}x^{n}$, the highest term of $fg$ is $a_{m}b_{n}x^{m+n}$, and $a_{m}b_{n} \ne 0$ because $R$ has no zero divisors. So $fg \ne 0$ and its degree is $m + n$. $\square$ It follows that the units of $F[x]$, for a field $F$, are exactly the nonzero constants: if $fg = 1$, the degrees add to $0$.

blocks.title: Multiplying in $\mathbb{Z}_{5}[x]$
blocks.q: Compute $(3x + 4)(2x^{2} + x + 3)$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{5}[x]$.

blocks.title: Degrees can drop
blocks.q: Compute $(2x + 1)(3x + 1)$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{6}[x]$.
steps: $6 \equiv 0$, so the product is $5x + 1$, of degree $1$, not $2$.
blocks.a: $5x + 1$: the leading coefficients $2$ and $3$ are zero divisors.

blocks.title: A strange unit
blocks.q: Show that $1 + 2x$ is a unit in $\mathbb{Z}_{4}[x]$.
steps: So $1 + 2x$ is its own inverse, a unit of degree $1$. This cannot happen over a field.

blocks.html: Counting. Over $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ a polynomial of degree at most $d$ has $d + 1$ coefficients, each with $p$ choices, so there are $p^{d+1}$ of them (including $0$); exactly $p^{d}$ are monic of degree $d$. These finite counts are what make $\mathbb{Z}_{p}[x]$ such a good laboratory.

Forgetting to reduce coefficients mod $n$, or trusting $\deg(fg) = \deg f + \deg g$ when the coefficients have zero divisors. In $\mathbb{Z}_{4}[x]$, $(2x + 1)(2x + 1) = 1$: two degree-1 polynomials with a product of degree $0$. The degree formula needs an integral domain such as $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$ or $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$.

$R[x]$ adds and multiplies polynomials with coefficients computed in $R$. Over an integral domain degrees add and $R[x]$ is again an integral domain; over $\mathbb{Z}_{n}$ with $n$ composite, degrees can drop and nonconstant units such as $1 + 2x$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{4}[x]$ appear.

blocks.html: Long division of polynomials works over any field, because each step divides by a leading coefficient. That single fact gives the remainder theorem, the factor theorem and a bound on the number of roots.

Division algorithm. Let $F$ be a field and $g \ne 0$ in $F[x]$. For every $f$ there are unique $q, r$ with $$f = qg + r, \qquad r = 0 \text{ or } \deg r \lt \deg g.$$ Existence: while $\deg f \ge \deg g$, subtract $\frac{a}{b}x^{m - n}g$, where $ax^{m}$ and $bx^{n}$ are the leading terms; this kills the leading term of $f$ and lowers its degree. (Here $\frac{a}{b}$ means $a$ times the inverse of $b$, which exists in a field.) Uniqueness: if $qg + r = q'g + r'$, then $(q - q')g = r' - r$; the right side has degree less than $\deg g$, so both sides are $0$. $\square$

Remainder and factor theorems. Dividing by $x - c$ leaves the constant $f(c)$ (substitute $x = c$ into $f = q(x)(x - c) + r$). So $c$ is a root exactly when $x - c$ divides $f$, as in algebra 2. Root bound: a nonzero polynomial of degree $n$ over a field (or integral domain) has at most $n$ roots, because each root splits off a factor $x - c$ and degrees add.

blocks.title: Dividing in $\mathbb{Z}_{3}[x]$
blocks.q: Divide $f = x^{3} + 2x + 1$ by $g = 2x + 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{3}[x]$.
steps: The leading coefficient of $g$ is $2$, and $2^{-1} = 2$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{3}$. First quotient term: $x^{3} \cdot 2 / x = 2x^{2}$. Subtract $2x^{2}(2x + 1) = 4x^{3} + 2x^{2} = x^{3} + 2x^{2}$: left $-2x^{2} + 2x + 1 = x^{2} + 2x + 1$.

blocks.title: Remainder without dividing
blocks.q: Find the remainder of $x^{4} + 2x^{2} + 5$ divided by $x - 3$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{7}[x]$.

blocks.title: Over $\mathbb{Q}$
blocks.q: Divide $2x^{3} - 3x^{2} + x + 5$ by $x - 2$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$.

blocks.html: Dividing by a leading coefficient as if you were in $\mathbb{Q}$: in $\mathbb{Z}_{3}$, "divide by 2" means multiply by $2^{-1} = 2$, never write $\frac{1}{2}$. And the root bound needs a field (or integral domain): in $\mathbb{Z}_{8}$, $x^{2} - 1$ has the four roots $1, 3, 5, 7$, because $(x - 3)(x - 5) = x^{2} - 8x + 15 = x^{2} - 1$ there too.

Division finds factors. A zero remainder hands you the factorization. Over $\mathbb{Z}_{5}$, dividing $x^{3} + 1$ by $x + 1$ leaves $(-1)^{3} + 1 = 0$, and the quotient gives $x^{3} + 1 = (x + 1)(x^{2} + 4x + 1)$.
Over a field, $f = qg + r$ with $\deg r \lt \deg g$, uniquely. Dividing by $x - c$ leaves $f(c)$, so $c$ is a root iff $(x - c) \mid f$, and a degree-$n$ polynomial has at most $n$ roots.

blocks.html: The Euclidean algorithm and Bézout's identity for integers carry over to polynomials word for word, because division with remainder works the same way. The payoff is a method for inverting elements of $F[x]/(p(x))$, the arithmetic of the new fields we are about to build.
Definition. Over a field $F$, $\gcd(f, g)$ is the monic common divisor of largest degree (monic makes it unique; any nonzero constant multiple divides just as well).

Euclidean algorithm. Divide $f = q_{1}g + r_{1}$, then $g = q_{2}r_{1} + r_{2}$, and so on; degrees drop each time, so a remainder eventually is $0$. The common divisors of $f$ and $g$ are the same as those of $g$ and $r_{1}$ (since $r_{1} = f - q_{1}g$), so the last nonzero remainder, made monic, is the gcd. Running the equations backward writes $$\gcd(f, g) = a(x)f(x) + b(x)g(x).$$ Inverses. If $p$ is irreducible and $p \nmid g$, then $\gcd(g, p) = 1 = ag + bp$, so $ag \equiv 1$ modulo $p$: the class of $a$ is the inverse of $g$ in $F[x]/(p)$.

blocks.title: A gcd in $\mathbb{Z}_{2}[x]$
steps: The last nonzero remainder is $x + 1$, already monic.

blocks.title: Over $\mathbb{Q}$ by factoring
blocks.q: Find the monic gcd of $f = 2(x - 1)(x - 2)(x + 3)$ and $g = (x - 1)(x + 3)(x + 4)$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$.
steps: The constant $2$ is a unit in $\mathbb{Q}$ and does not count.

blocks.title: An inverse in a quotient ring
blocks.q: In $\mathbb{Z}_{2}[x]/(x^{3} + x + 1)$, find the inverse of $x$.
steps: So $1 = (x^{3} + x + 1) - (x^{2} + 1)x$, and modulo $x^{3} + x + 1$ this says $(x^{2} + 1)x \equiv -1 = 1$.

blocks.html: One structural consequence: in $F[x]$ every ideal is generated by one polynomial (take a nonzero element of least degree and divide), just as every ideal of $\mathbb{Z}$ is $(n)$. Rings with this property are called principal ideal domains.

Forgetting to make the gcd monic (over $\mathbb{Z}_{5}$, $3x + 1$ and $x + 2$ are the same gcd up to the unit $3$; the answer is the monic one, $x + 2$), or reporting the last remainder, $0$, instead of the one before it.

Why the gcd decides invertibility. Let $g \ne 0$ have degree less than $\deg p$. In $F[x]/(p)$, $g$ has an inverse exactly when $\gcd(g, p) = 1$. If $ag + bp = 1$, then $ag \equiv 1$. If instead $d = \gcd(g, p)$ has positive degree, then $g \cdot \frac{p}{d} = \frac{g}{d} \cdot p \equiv 0$ with $\frac{p}{d} \not\equiv 0$, so $g$ is a zero divisor and has no inverse.

The Euclidean algorithm finds $\gcd(f, g)$ in $F[x]$ (made monic),
 and running it backward gives $\gcd = af + bg$. When $\gcd(g, p) = 1$, the coefficient $a$ is the inverse of $g$ modulo $p$.

blocks.html: Irreducible polynomials play the role of primes in $F[x]$, and they are exactly what we need to build fields ($F[x]/(f)$ is a field when $f$ is irreducible, by the maximal ideal theorem). For small degrees there is a quick test.

Definition. A polynomial $f \in F[x]$ of degree at least $1$ is irreducible over $F$ if it is not a product of two polynomials of lower degree. Irreducibility depends on the field: $x^{2} - 2$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ but equals $(x - \sqrt{2})(x + \sqrt{2})$ over $\mathbb{R}$.

Degree 2 and 3. A polynomial of degree $2$ or $3$ over a field is irreducible exactly when it has no root in the field.
Proof. If it factors, the degrees of the factors add to $2$ or $3$, so one factor has degree $1$, say $a(x - c)$, and then $c$ is a root. Conversely, a root $c$ gives the factor $x - c$. $\square$ For degree $4$ and up this fails: a product of two irreducible quadratics has no roots.

Over $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ you can test every element. There are $\frac{p^{2} - p}{2}$ monic irreducible quadratics over $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$: of the $p^{2}$ monic quadratics, the reducible ones are $(x - a)(x - b)$, and there are $p$ with $a = b$ plus $\binom{p}{2}$ with $a \ne b$.

blocks.title: The same polynomial, two fields
blocks.q: Is $x^{2} + 1$ irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}_{3}$? Over $\mathbb{Z}_{5}$?

blocks.title: Irreducibles over $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$
blocks.q: Find all irreducible polynomials of degree $2$ and $3$ over $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$.
steps: A root in $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ is $0$ or $1$. No root at $0$ means constant term $1$; no root at $1$ means an odd number of nonzero terms.

blocks.title: Degree 4 needs more
blocks.q: $x^{4} + x^{2} + 1$ has no root in $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$. Is it irreducible?
steps: Check the only irreducible quadratic: $(x^{2} + x + 1)^{2} = x^{4} + 2x^{3} + 3x^{2} + 2x + 1 = x^{4} + x^{2} + 1$ (mod 2).

blocks.html: Applying the root test to degree $4$. Over $\mathbb{R}$, $x^{4} + 2x^{2} + 1 = (x^{2} + 1)^{2}$ has no real root but is reducible. For degree $4$ you must also rule out a product of two quadratics, for example by dividing by each irreducible quadratic.
In degree $2$ or $3$, irreducible over a field means no root in the field; over $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ just test every element. From degree $4$ on, also check for quadratic factors.

blocks.html: Over $\mathbb{Q}$ you cannot test every number for a root. Instead there are tools that use integer arithmetic. Together they settle most polynomials you will meet. They start from the rational root theorem and build on the degree-2-or-3 test.

items: Rational root test. If $\frac{r}{s}$ in lowest terms is a root of $a_{n}x^{n} + \cdots + a_{0}$ with integer coefficients, then $r \mid a_{0}$ and $s \mid a_{n}$. For degree $2$ or $3$, no rational root means irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$.
Gauss's lemma. If a polynomial with integer coefficients factors over $\mathbb{Q}$, it factors into polynomials with integer coefficients of the same degrees. So we may work in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.

Eisenstein's criterion. If a prime $p$ divides every coefficient except the leading one, does not divide the leading coefficient, and $p^{2}$ does not divide the constant term, then the polynomial is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$.

Reduction mod $p$. If $p$ does not divide the leading coefficient and the reduction mod $p$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ (of the same degree), then the polynomial is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$.

blocks.html: Why Eisenstein works. Suppose $f = gh$ in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ (Gauss's lemma) with both factors of positive degree, and reduce mod $p$. All coefficients of $f$ but the leading one vanish, so $\bar{f} = \bar{a}_{n}x^{n}$. Since $\mathbb{Z}_{p}[x]$ has unique factorization, $\bar{g}$ and $\bar{h}$ must also be monomials $\bar{b}x^{k}$ and $\bar{c}x^{n-k}$ with $k, n - k \ge 1$ (their degrees cannot drop, because $p$ does not divide the leading coefficient of $f$). So $p$ divides the constant terms of both $g$ and $h$, and $p^{2}$ divides their product, the constant term of $f$: a contradiction. $\square$ Why reduction works: a factorization $f = gh$ over $\mathbb{Z}$ reduces to a factorization $\bar{f} = \bar{g}\bar{h}$ of the same shape.

blocks.title: Eisenstein
blocks.q: Show that $x^{4} + 10x + 5$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$.
steps: Take $p = 5$: $5$ divides $10$ and $5$ (and the zero coefficients), $5 \nmid 1$, and $25 \nmid 5$.

blocks.title: A cubic
blocks.q: Is $x^{3} - 3x - 1$ irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$?
steps: No rational root, and a cubic with no root is irreducible.
blocks.a: Irreducible. (Eisenstein does not apply to it at any prime.)

blocks.title: A shift makes Eisenstein work
blocks.q: Show that $f(x) = x^{4} + x^{3} + x^{2} + x + 1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$.
steps: A factorization of $f(x)$ would give one of $f(x + 1)$, so $f$ is irreducible.

blocks.title: Reduction mod 2
blocks.q: Show that $x^{3} + 3x + 7$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$.
steps: Mod $2$ it becomes $x^{3} + x + 1$, which has no root in $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ ($f(0) = 1$, $f(1) = 1$), so it is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$.
The leading coefficient $1$ is not divisible by $2$, so $x^{3} + 3x + 7$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$.

blocks.html: Treating a failed test as a proof of reducibility. If Eisenstein does not apply at any prime, or the reduction mod $3$ factors, that proves nothing: $x^{3} - 3x - 1$ above is irreducible although Eisenstein fails. Also never reduce mod a prime that divides the leading coefficient: $2x^{2} + x$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is reducible ($x(2x + 1)$), but mod $2$ it becomes $x$, of lower degree.

Over $\mathbb{Q}$: rational root test (enough in degree 2 or 3), Eisenstein's criterion (possibly after a shift $x \mapsto x + 1$), and reduction mod a prime not dividing the leading coefficient. A test that fails proves nothing.
